small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Autumn_Foundation_Algebraic manipulation_1_Substitution
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students consolidate their understanding and application of substituting given values into algebraic expressions and formulae. It is important for students to practise substituting values into a wide variety of expressions and formulae, including those with coefficients, exponents, multiple terms, and fractions. They should also work with a mixture of values, such as integers, negative numbers, decimals and fractions. Ensure that students practise substitution with and without a calculator. When using a calculator, highlight that, for example evaluating 3a2 when a = 4, can be calculated by typing 3 × 42 or 3(4)2

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Autumn_Foundation_Algebraic manipulation_2_Collect like terms
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students identify like terms in expressions and simplify by adding or subtracting like terms. Students will recap their understanding of collecting like terms from Key Stage 3. Remind students that like terms include the same variables to the same power, for example, a and 3a are like terms but 3a and 2a2 are not. Include examples of terms with a coefficient of 1 and discuss the convention of writing these as, for example, c rather than 1c. Include terms with squared or multiple variables, for example, t2 or 4ab, and discuss the commutative properties of like terms, such as 3pq and 3qp. Encourage students to use the ‘≡’ symbol to indicate that the original and simplified expressions are equivalent.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Autumn_Foundation_Algebraic manipulation_3_Simplify expressions
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students simplify expressions using multiplication and division, building on their knowledge from Key Stage 3. Remind students that 7 × c is equivalent to 7c and c 3 is equivalent to c ÷ 3 Students should practise simplifying expressions that involve a fraction or division, which will require them to, at times, identify common numerical and/or simple algebraic factors. Begin by ensuring students are confident in simplifying expressions such as 5 × a × a and a × b ÷ 2 before progressing to more complex expressions. Students should also be confident that a × a should be written as a2. Students will look at laws of indices later within this block, and powers greater than 2 are not explored in this step. Remind students that the process of simplifying an expression maintains equivalence.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Autumn_Foundation_Algebraic manipulation_4_Addition and subtraction laws for indices
small_step_name: Addition and subtraction laws for indices
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students recap the addition and subtraction laws of indices, building on learning from Year 8. Remind students that ax × ay ≡ ax + y and a a x y ≡ ax – y. It is important for students to note that to apply these laws, the base must be the same. Students should be familiar with questions involving both numerical bases, for example, 23 × 25 and algebraic bases, for example x4 × x7 Students should initially start with expressions with a coefficient of 1, before moving to expressions with greater coefficients. As confidence develops, progress students on to more complex expressions, including multiple variables, for example 12 4 5 3 x y x

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Autumn_Foundation_Algebraic manipulation_5_Powers of powers
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students build on their understanding of the laws of indices and now look at powers of powers. Students may have covered this previously in Year 8 as an extend step. Begin exploring examples such as (x3)2 and discussing how this represents “x3 squared”, which is equivalent to x3 multiplied by x3. This allows students to use their understanding of the addition law of indices to make connections to explain why (x3)2 ≡ x6. Encourage students to generalise by repeating with other expressions. Once students are confident, progress to expressions that include coefficients of the variable, for example (3x4)2. If appropriate, challenge students to consider examples such as 22 × 45, where they need to adapt a value, so they have the same base, for example 22 × (22)5

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Autumn_Foundation_Algebraic manipulation_6_Expand a single bracket
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students recap expanding a single bracket, building on their learning from Key Stage 3. Ensure students are confident in expanding brackets in the form a(bx + c) and ax(bx + c) including expressions with negative values of a, b and c. Once students are confident, begin to introduce expressions including indices, for example, 3x(x2 + 4). It may be necessary to recap the laws of indices and simplifying expressions from the previous steps with students. Algebra tiles can be used to support students’ understanding, where necessary and appropriate. Students will also recap expanding and simplifying single brackets in the form a(x ± b) ± c(x ± d) and a ± b(x ± c). Introduce expressions that include both positive and negative coefficients of the variable. Use terminology such as “multiply out” and “expand” for command words in questions to align with wording from exam boards.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Autumn_Foundation_Algebraic manipulation_7_Factorise into a single bracket
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students recap factorising expressions into single brackets, building on their learning from Key Stage 3. It can be useful to revisit finding the highest common factor of a variety of terms, including those where the highest common factor is algebraic. small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Autumn_Foundation_Equations inequalities and formulae_1_Solve equations
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students revisit solving 1- and 2-step equations, which were covered in Key Stage 3, before moving on to more complex equations later in the block. small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Autumn_Foundation_Equations inequalities and formulae_6_Change the subject of a simple formula
small_step_name: Change the subject of a simple formula
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students rearrange simple formulae that involve one or two steps of working, to change the subject. Note that this may be the first time students have changed the subject of a formula, as this is not covered in the Key Stage 3 Support curriculum. Bar models and function machines can be useful representations to support students’ understanding. Drawing comparisons to solving equations is useful as students begin to explore this concept. Ensure that students understand the subject of a formula is the variable that is isolated and equal to an expression involving other variables. Discuss the fact that the subject of a formula can appear on either the left or right side of the equals sign. For example, r is the subject of both r = m + p and m + p = r.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Autumn_Foundation_Equations inequalities and formulae_7_Change the subject of a known formula
small_step_name: Change the subject of a known formula
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students rearrange known formulae, building on learning from Key Stage 3. Students use rearrangements of formulae to solve problems, such as making d the subject of C = πd to work out the diameter of a circle when given the circumference. For example, writing A = 1 2 bh as A = bh 2 to highlight that both sides of the formula can be multiplied by 2 as a first step to make b or h the subject.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Autumn_Foundation_Expand double brackets_1_Factorise quadratic expressions (positive only)
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students will build on their knowledge of expanding double brackets in the form (ax ± b)(cx ± d) from Key Stage 3. Begin with expressions in the form (x + a)(x + b), with all positive terms, and introduce negative terms as students’ confidence develops, before introducing expressions with coefficients of the variable. Expressions in unfamiliar forms such as (x + 2)2 or (x + 2)(3 + x) can also be explored. Recap the use of an area model as a visual prompt for discussion on how to expand binomials, using algebra tiles to support if necessary. Students need to be confident with simplification and calculating with negative numbers. Where appropriate, extend students by expanding brackets in other mathematical contexts, for example, expressing the area of rectilinear shapes with binomial dimensions.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Autumn_Foundation_Expand double brackets_2_Factorise quadratic expressions
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students will factorise quadratic expressions in the form x2 + bx + c, which they may have previously explored in Key Stage 3. Students will look at factorising expressions including negatives in the following step. Begin by asking students to find two numbers that make a specific sum and product, for example, find two numbers that have a sum of 7 and a product of 10 Support students to make connections by explicitly showing that factorising is the inverse of expanding brackets. Using algebra tiles and multiplication grids can strengthen students’ conceptual understanding.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Autumn_Foundation_Expand double brackets_3_Difference of two squares (E)
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students will factorise quadratic expressions in the form x2 ± bx ± c. This will build on students’ understanding from the previous step of factorising expressions in the form x2 + bx + c. In this step, it may be useful to recap calculations with directed numbers. Similarly to the last step, begin by asking students to find two numbers that make a specific sum and product, for example, find two numbers that have a sum of –6 and a product of 8, and encourage students to factorise an expression using these values, for example, x2 – 6x + 8 Using algebra tiles and multiplication grids can strengthen students’ conceptual understanding. Once students are confident, progress onto factorising expressions such as x2 + 7x – 30 and x2 – x – 12

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Autumn_Foundation_Expand double brackets_4_Solve quadratic equations equal to 0
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students will explore expressions in the form x2 – a2 where a is an integer. Encourage students to expand brackets of the form (x ± a)(x ± a) to uncover the difference of two squares and explore the connection to quadratics in the form x2 ± bx ± c, noting how the middle term bx is eliminated. This exploration should help them make the link before moving onto factorisation. Highlight to students that, for example, in the expression x2 – 36, the value of b is 0, hence why it is omitted. Then encourage students to consider a factor pair of –36 that sum to 0, to enable them to factorise the expression. Repeat with other expressions in this form, encouraging students to spot that the value of c is always a square number. If appropriate, explore fully factorising expressions such as 48 – 3y2

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Autumn_Foundation_Expand double brackets_5_Solve quadratic equations by factorisation
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students will solve quadratic expressions equal to zero in the form (x + a)(x + b) = 0. The purpose of this step is to prepare students for solving quadratic equations by factorisation. Firstly, practise solving linear equations equal to zero such as x + 2 = 0 and ab = 0, varying the value of a or b before solving. Draw students’ attention to the fact that if the product of two numbers or terms is zero, then at least one of the two numbers or terms must be zero. This understanding helps explain why quadratic equations can have up to two solutions. Remind students that (x + a)(x + b) = 0 represents (x + a) × (x + b) = 0, and so to solve it, the value of either bracket must be 0

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Autumn_Foundation_Expand double brackets_6_Quadratic graphs of the form y = x2 + a
small_step_name: Quadratic graphs of the form y = x2 + a
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students will solve quadratic equations by first factorising the equation. Students may be familiar with solving quadratic equations from Year 9, as this was previously covered as an extend step. Building on students’ understanding from the previous step, begin with factorising quadratic equations that are equal to zero before asking students to solve. Emphasise that quadratic equations must be equal to zero before they can be factorised. Encourage students to check their solutions by substituting into the original equation. Once students are confident, challenge them to solve quadratic equations that are not equal to zero and require rearranging before solving, for example, x2 + 7x = –12 Make links between solving a quadratic and the graphical representation of the quadratic using dynamic software.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Autumn_Foundation_Percentages_1_Percentage of an amount
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students find percentages of an amount using both calculator and non-calculator methods. Students need to be confident with both and would benefit from having a bank of different methods for each to support them answering a variety of different question types. A good discussion point is around which method is most appropriate and efficient in each scenario. Start by finding different percentages of simple numbers to focus on methods before increasing arithmetic complexity by using more challenging percentages and numbers. The use of multipliers supports efficiency by using a single calculation and supports students with later steps in the block. Students that followed the Support Curriculum in Year 9 may not be familiar with using multipliers to calculate percentages. This step also provides an opportunity to incorporate contextual links, such as working out the amount of tax a person pays.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Autumn_Foundation_Percentages_2_Percentage increase and decrease
baseline_ss_wr_desc: Building on from the previous small step, students use calculator and non-calculator methods to increase and decrease by a given percentage. If students followed the Support Curriculum in Year 9, they may have only increased or decreased with percentages that are multiples of 5%. baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students will learn how to represent the solutions to inequalities using formal set notation. Students will make links between number line representations, verbal descriptions and formal set notation. Highlight that a colon in set notation can be interpreted as “such that”. Representing these on a number line is a useful visual aid to highlight values that do not satisfy these inequalities.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Autumn_Higher_Equations inequalities and formulae_9_Change the subject of a complex formula
small_step_name: Change the subject of a complex formula
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students rearrange complex formulae involving combinations of squares, square roots, fractions and brackets. Explore strategies to rearrange formulae where the proposed subject has a negative coefficient, such as making t the subject of y = x – t. Comparing this to solving a “subtract from” equation such as 5 = 12 – t could be useful. Students could then move on to formulae like this involving fractions. Once students are confident, introduce formulae involving brackets, while comparing different strategies, such as expanding a bracket or dividing by the coefficient of the bracket. Students should also be given opportunities to rearrange formulae with squared terms and/or respective roots.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Autumn_Higher_Expand double brackets_10_Solve quadratic equations by completing the square (E)
small_step_name: Solve quadratic equations by completing the square (E)
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students will complete the square with quadratic expressions in the form ax2 ± bx ± c where a > 1 and rewrite them in the form a(x ± p)2 ± q. Remind students how to complete the square for quadratic expressions where the coefficient of x2 is 1 Direct students to factor out the coefficient of x2, to bring a sense of familiarity from the previous step of completing the square, before expanding by the factorised coefficient of x2 Highlight to students the use of square brackets here to separate the different factorisations. As students’ confidence grows, introduce expressions where all terms are not a factor of the coefficient of x2 and the use of fractional terms is necessary, such as 2x2 + 4x – 3 ≡ 2 x2 + 2x – 3 2

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Autumn_Higher_Expand double brackets_11_Solve quadratic equations using the quadratic formula
small_step_name: Solve quadratic equations using the quadratic formula
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students will solve quadratic equations by completing the square. This step builds on students’ understanding of solving equations from the previous block and the process of completing the square. Ensure students are confident solving equations involving squared terms, negative values, and fractions. Begin with expressions in the form x2 + bx + c = 0, where b is a positive even number, to reinforce the method. Then, as students develop confidence, introduce negative and odd coefficients of x. Remind students that when trying to solve equations such as x2 = 16, there are both positive and negative roots, which is why quadratic equations often have two solutions. Model leaving solutions in exact form as well as rounded answers from a calculator. Encourage students to consider when it may be necessary to complete the square instead of factorising when solving quadratics.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Autumn_Higher_Expand double brackets_1_Expand triple brackets
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students will build on their knowledge of expanding double brackets in the form (ax ± b)(cx ± d) from Key Stage 3. Begin with expressions in the form (x + a)(x + b), with all positive terms, and introduce negative terms as students’ confidence develops, before introducing expressions with coefficients of the variable. Expressions in unfamiliar forms such as (x + 2)2 or (x + 2)(3 + x) can also be explored. Recap the use of an area model as a visual prompt for discussion on how to expand binomials, using algebra tiles to support if necessary. Students need to be confident with simplification and calculating with negative numbers. Where appropriate, extend students by expanding brackets in other mathematical contexts, for example, expressing the area of rectilinear shapes with binomial dimensions.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Autumn_Higher_Expand double brackets_2_Factorise quadratic expressions
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students explore expanding triple brackets in the form (ax ± b)(cx ± d)(ex ± f). Students may have previously encountered this topic as an extend step in Year 9 Build on their knowledge of expanding double brackets by systematically modelling the expansion and simplification of the first two brackets before expanding the result by the third bracket. Using a multiplication grid can help students organise their work and ensure all terms are included. Encourage students to check that every term is multiplied. As their confidence develops, introduce negative terms and other triple-bracket formats such as (x + 2)3 and (x – 2)2(3 + x).

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Autumn_Higher_Expand double brackets_3_Factorise more complex quadratic expressions (E)
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students will factorise quadratic expressions in the form x2 ± bx ± c. Students may have previously covered this in Key Stage 3. Support students to make connections by explicitly showing that factorising is the inverse of expanding brackets. Begin by asking students to find two numbers that make a specific sum and product, for example, find two numbers that have a sum of 7 and a product of 10 Students should first factorise expressions in the form x2 + bx + c. Once students are confident, progress onto factorising expressions such as x2 + 7x – 30 and x2 – x – 12 Using algebra tiles and multiplication grids can strengthen students’ conceptual understanding.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Autumn_Higher_Expand double brackets_4_Difference of two squares
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students will factorise quadratic expressions of the form ax2 ± bx ± c where a > 1. Emphasise that they need to consider both the factors of the x2 coefficient and the factors of the constant term when factorising. Start with expressions where a is a prime number. Using algebra tiles can support understanding, allowing students to determine the correct factor pairs for a and c that will sum to b when expanded. As confidence develops, students can progress to a more abstract method, using trial and improvement to find the correct factor pairs. Draw students’ attention to how the position of the factors within the bracket affects the final answer, for example (3x + 4)(2x + 5) is different to (3x + 5)(2x + 4). Encourage students to expand the brackets afterwards to check their factorisation.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Autumn_Higher_Expand double brackets_5_Solve quadratic equations equal to 0
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students will explore expressions in the form x2 – a2 where a is an integer. Encourage students to expand brackets of the form (x ± a)(x ± a) to uncover the difference of two squares. Explore the connection to quadratics in the form x2 ± bx ± c, noting how the middle term bx is eliminated. Highlight to students that, for example, in the expression x2 – 36, the value of b is 0, hence why it is omitted. Then encourage students to consider a factor pair of –36 that sum to 0, to enable them to factorise the expression. Repeat with other expressions in this form, encouraging students to spot that the value of c is always a square number. Once students are confident, challenge them to factorise expressions like 4x2 – 25 If appropriate, explore fully factorising expressions such as 48 – 3y2

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Autumn_Higher_Expand double brackets_6_Solve quadratic equations by factorisation
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students will solve quadratic expressions equal to zero in the form (x + a)(x + b) = 0. The purpose of this step is to prepare students for solving quadratic equations by factorisation. Firstly, practise solving linear equations equal to zero such as x + 2 = 0 and ab = 0, varying the value of a or b before solving. Draw students’ attention to the fact that if the product of two numbers or terms is zero, then at least one of the two numbers or terms must be zero. This understanding helps explain why quadratic equations can have up to two solutions. Remind students that (x + a)(x + b) = 0 represents (x + a) × (x + b) = 0, and so to solve it, the value of either bracket must be 0 Once students are confident, progress to solving equations with coefficients of x, for example, (3x + 4)(2x – 1).

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Autumn_Higher_Expand double brackets_7_Solve more complex quadratic equations by factorisation (E)
small_step_name: Solve more complex quadratic equations by factorisation (E)
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students will solve quadratic equations by first factorising the equation. Students may be familiar with solving quadratic equations from Year 9, as this was previously covered as an extend step. Building on students’ understanding from the previous step, begin with factorising quadratic equations that are equal to zero before asking students to solve. Emphasise that quadratic equations must be equal to zero before they can be solved by factorisation. Encourage students to check their solutions by substituting into the original equation. Once students are confident, challenge them to solve quadratic equations that are not equal to zero and require rearranging before solving, for example, x2 + 7x = –12 Make links between solving a quadratic and the graphical representation of the quadratic using dynamic software.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Autumn_Higher_Expand double brackets_8_Complete the square
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students will solve quadratics by first factorising expressions in the form ax2 ± bx ± c. This will build on students’ understanding of solving quadratic equations from the previous step, but it will now incorporate those where the coefficient of x2 is greater than 1 Encourage students to form equations for each bracket. For example, (3x + 4)(2x – 1) = 0 can be solved using 3x + 4 = 0 and 2x – 1 = 0 before solving these separately to find the solutions of x. Encourage students to check their solutions by substituting into the original expression. Once students are confident, challenge them to solve expressions that require rearranging. For example, 4x2 + 10x + 8 = 6 + 3x – x2

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Autumn_Higher_Expand double brackets_9_Complete the square with more complex quadratic expressions (E)
small_step_name: Complete the square with more complex quadratic expressions (E)
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students will complete the square with quadratic expressions in the form x2 ± bx ± c by writing them in the form (x ± p)2 ± q. It is useful to begin by showing students examples of expressions that form a perfect square, for example, how x2 + 6x + 9 can be factorised to (x + 3)2 Remind students that not all quadratic expressions can be factorised this way, but completing the square allows any quadratic expression to be rewritten as a single bracket squared, +/– a constant. Use algebra tiles to demonstrate the “square” and visualise why the coefficient of x is halved to find p and how to determine the value of q. Begin with expressions that have all positive terms and an even coefficient of x before introducing negative coefficients and odd coefficients of x. Discuss with students how completing the square can later be applied to solve quadratic equations and to find the turning point of a quadratic graph. These topics will be covered later this year.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Autumn_Higher_Percentages_1_Percentage of an amount
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students find percentages of an amount using both calculator and non-calculator methods. Students need to be confident with both and would benefit from having a bank of different methods for each to support them answering a variety of different question types. A good discussion point is around which method is most appropriate and efficient in each scenario, although this can be discussed retrospectively if students would benefit more from just completing the calculations initially. Start by finding different percentages of simple numbers to focus on methods before increasing arithmetic complexity by using more challenging percentages and numbers. The use of multipliers supports efficiency by using a single calculation and supports students with later steps in the block. This step also provides an opportunity to incorporate contextual links, such as working out the amount of tax a person pays.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Autumn_Higher_Percentages_3_Repeated percentage change
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students explore repeated percentage change involving both percentage increases and decreases. This will support students when later exploring compound interest, which is a specific example of repeated percentage change. Examples should include those where the percentage an amount is increasing or decreasing by remains constant, and also examples where it changes. Students should also explore growth and decay problems. Multipliers are the most efficient method when the repeated change is with the same percentage. For example, a 5% increase followed by a 10% increase is not equivalent to a 15% increase of the original value.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Autumn_Higher_Percentages_4_Express one number as a fraction or percentage of another
small_step_name: Express one number as a fraction or percentage of another
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students express one number as a fraction or a percentage of another using both calculator and non-calculator methods. It is useful to start with fractions, as students’ common terminology around fractions will support their understanding. For example, 11 50 is often read as “eleven fiftieths” or “11 out of 50”, and the latter supports this learning. Once confident in this, students can then use their understanding of percentages being out of 100 and equivalent fractions to express one number as a percentage of another, before moving on to more complex examples where they express any number as a fraction or percentage of another. Encourage students to check their answers by calculating the fraction or percentage of the amount to ensure it is accurate.

Encourage students to solve using the quadratic formula both with and without a calculator by breaking down the calculation, step-by-step, as this minimises errors. Encourage students to use brackets when substituting, especially with negatives. If appropriate, discuss aspects of the quadratic formula such as the discriminant, but note that this is not explicitly covered until A-level.

Students may be familiar with solving quadratic equations from Year 9, as this was previously covered as an extend step. Building on students' understanding from the previous step, begin with factorising quadratic equations that are equal to zero before asking students to solve. Emphasise that quadratic equations must be equal to zero before they can be solved by factorisation. Encourage students to check their solutions by substituting into the original equation. Once students are confident, challenge them to solve quadratic equations that are not equal to zero and require rearranging before solving, for example, x2 + 7x = –12. Make links between solving a quadratic and the graphical representation of the quadratic using dynamic software.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Autumn_Higher_Quadratic expressions and equations_8_Complete the square
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students will solve quadratics by first factorising expressions in the form ax2 ± bx ± c. This will build on students' understanding of solving quadratic equations from the previous step, but it will now incorporate those where the coefficient of x2 is greater than 1. Encourage students to form equations for each bracket. For example, (3x + 4)(2x – 1) = 0 can be solved using 3x + 4 = 0 and 2x – 1 = 0 before solving these separately to find the solutions of x. Encourage students to check their solutions by substituting into the original expression. Once students are confident, challenge them to solve expressions that require rearranging. For example, 4x2 + 10x + 8 = 6 + 3x – x2.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Autumn_Higher_Quadratic expressions and equations_9_Complete the square with more complex quadratic expressions (E)
small_step_name: Complete the square with more complex quadratic expressions (E)
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students will complete the square with quadratic expressions in the form x2 ± bx ± c by writing them in the form (x ± p)2 ± q. It is useful to begin by showing students examples of expressions that form a perfect square, for example, how x2 + 6x + 9 can be factorised to (x + 3)2. Remind students that not all quadratic expressions can be factorised this way, but completing the square allows any quadratic expression to be rewritten as a single bracket squared, +/– a constant. Use algebra tiles to demonstrate the "square" and visualise why the coefficient of x is halved to find p and how to determine the value of q. Begin with expressions that have all positive terms and an even coefficient of x before introducing negative coefficients and odd coefficients of x. Discuss with students how completing the square can later be applied to solve quadratic equations and to find the turning point of a quadratic graph. These topics will be covered later this year.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Autumn_Higher_Ratio and scale_1_Equivalent ratios
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students find equivalent ratios and simplify ratios, building on their learning from Key Stage 3. Remind students to identify the highest common factor of the numbers in a given ratio and highlight that dividing by the highest common factor will give a ratio in its simplest form. Other strategies can also be explored, such as dividing the ratio 24 : 18 by 2, and then by 3. Ensure that students understand that equivalent ratios are multiples or factors of each other and discuss how to work out equivalent ratios, for example by doubling both numbers in a given ratio. Discuss with students how ratios involving units such as money, time or length need to be re-written using the same units before they can be simplified. If appropriate, students could explore writing ratios in the form 1 : n or n : 1. Note that this is an extend step in Year 8, so some students may not have covered this before.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Autumn_Higher_Ratio and scale_3_Link ratios and fractions
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students explore how the parts in a ratio compare to each value in the ratio as a fraction of the whole, building on learning from Year 8. Single bar models can be useful for highlighting the differences between fractions and ratios. Remind students that a ratio compares one part of a whole to another part, whereas a fraction compares one part to the whole. Provide students with the opportunity to write a ratio as a fraction and a fraction as a ratio. Students should also be given opportunities to use fractions to compare ratios, such as the ratio of water to juice in two different drinks to decide which is stronger. Students may need to revisit strategies for comparing fractions, such as writing equivalent fractions and comparing the numerators when the denominators are the same.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Autumn_Higher_Ratio and scale_4_Combine a set of ratios
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students use their knowledge of equivalent ratios to combine two ratios. Remind students how to identify the lowest common multiple of two numbers and ensure that they can work with equivalent ratios. Support students by modelling the use of language such as “for every red, there are yellow”. In addition, encourage students to identify common parts between ratios. For example, the ratios red : blue and blue : yellow both include “blue”. Highlight that the common parts in ratios must be equal to combine them and explore methods for this, such as scaling one of the given ratios. Extra challenge can be added by changing the common term. For example, providing the ratios red : blue and red : yellow.

baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students make links between scales on a map or diagram and ratios. small_step_name: Mean from a grouped frequency table
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students estimate the mean from grouped frequency tables. This may have previously been covered in Year 8 as an extend step. Begin by reviewing how to calculate the mean from raw data to highlight the difference when working with grouped data. Emphasise that when data is grouped, individual values are unknown, so the mean can only be estimated. Explain that the midpoint of each interval is used as a representative value, assuming an even distribution within each group. Model the process step by step, showing how to identify midpoints, multiply them by their corresponding frequencies, sum these products, and divide by the total frequency to find an estimated mean.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Spring_Foundation_Interpret and represent data_7_Sampling
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students develop their understanding of data collection by exploring sampling, a method used to gather information from part of a population when it isn’t practical to survey everyone. Begin by defining the population as the entire group being studied, such as all students in a school, and a sample as a smaller group representing it. Introduce random sampling, where each individual has an equal chance of being selected, and systematic sampling, where selections are made at regular intervals. Once students are confident, explore stratified sampling, where the population is divided into groups (strata) and a proportional sample is taken from each. Encourage students to apply proportional reasoning to calculate sample sizes and discuss which method is most reliable in different situations. Emphasise the importance of avoiding bias when selecting samples.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Spring_Foundation_Interpret and represent data_8_Scatter graphs
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students review scatter graphs, building on their prior knowledge from Key Stage 3. The focus is on reinforcing key vocabulary such as “positive correlation”, “negative correlation” and “no correlation”, and developing confidence in interpreting the relationship between two variables from the graph. Draw students’ attention to how the direction and strength of the pattern suggest different types of correlation. Students should also practise drawing a line of best fit and using it to make simple estimates. It is worth noting that, while lines of best fit in maths are straight lines, they may be curved in science depending on the nature of the data. It is valuable to remind students that correlation does not imply causality, and that the absence of a clear linear relationship does not necessarily mean the variables are unconnected.

This helps students appreciate that extrapolation relies on assumptions and reinforces the importance of applying mathematical models carefully and critically.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Spring_Foundation_Non-calculator methods_6_Order of operations
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students develop their understanding of how to priortise operations in calculations, including those with directed number. Acronyms such as BIDMAS or BODMAS may be misleading as they imply that each operation has its own place in priority. Instead, highlight that some operations have equal priority, for example multiplication and division. Draw students’ attention to examples where operations should be calculated from left to right, for example, when calculating 20 – 5 + 3, 20 – 5 should be calculated first. Ensure students have opportunities to explore calculations involving all four operations, as well as powers and brackets throughout the step. Most calculators use order of operations correctly, but comparing and checking answers is useful.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Spring_Foundation_Non-calculator methods_7_Related calculations
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students use known numerical facts to derive other related facts. Students will make links between similar calculations, for example, understanding that if 12 × 9 = 108 then 1.2 × 0.9 = 1.08. Attention should be drawn to how the numbers in a calculation have been manipulated and the effect this will have on a given answer. For example, if both numbers in a multiplication are multiplied by 10, then the new product will be 100 times greater than the original product. Students must also understand that this logic does not apply to division. For example, if both numbers in a division are multiplied by 10, then the new product will be the same as the original product. For division, this can be linked to students’ understanding of equivalent fractions, for example, 45 ÷ 0.5 = 45 0.5 = 90 1 = 90

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Spring_Foundation_Non-linear graphs_2_Intercepts and roots of quadratic graphs (E)
small_step_name: Intercepts and roots of quadratic graphs (E)
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students identify and interpret the roots and intercepts of quadratic graphs, reinforcing connections to their previous work on solving quadratics. Begin by exploring examples where the roots and y-intercept can be identified through inspection before introducing algebraic methods. Emphasise that the roots of the equation y = ax2 + bx + c correspond to the solutions of ax2 + bx + c = 0 and should be written in the form x = d. Remind students that the y-intercept can be found by substituting x = 0 into the equation to identify the value of y before writing as a coordinate in the form (0, y). Provide opportunities for students to explore graphs that have 0, 1 or 2 roots, helping them recognise how the number of solutions relates to the graph’s intersection with the x-axis. Dynamic graphing software can be used to support understanding.

Challenge students to work backwards to calculate an unknown side length when the total surface area is given.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Spring_Foundation_Probability_4_Relative frequency
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students consolidate their understanding from Key Stage 3, to consider relative frequency as a form of experimental probability. Students should recognise that probability is often considered in theoretical terms, where predictions are made about events that have not yet happened, while relative frequency is based on data from experiments or past events. Comparing theoretical probability with relative frequency can strengthen students’ understanding. A key discussion point is the effect of the number of trials on accuracy. Students should see that as the number of trials increases, the relative frequency tends to approach the theoretical probability. Students will also estimate the expected number of outcomes of an event using the relative frequency.

baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students revisit independent events, first introduced in Key Stage 3. Distinguishing between independent and dependent events can be a challenging concept, so it is important to spend time ensuring students can recognise the difference. small_step_name: Find solutions to equations using straight lines graphs
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students use straight-line graphs to solve related equations. Remind students how to identify points that lie on pairs of lines, for example, how to verify the point (2, 6) lies on the lines y = 3x and y = 6. Build on this to show students how to solve an equation graphically. For example, solving 2x – 7 = 8 by drawing the graphs of y = 2x – 7 and y = 8 and identifying the x-coordinate of the point of intersection as the solution to the equation. small_step_name: Find the equation of a line from a graph (E)

Challenge students by working with fractional and negative values.

Challenge students to solve more complex problems involving midpoints and 2-D shapes.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Spring_Higher_Interpret and represent data_10_Interpolation and extrapolation
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students use scatter graphs to make predictions, with particular emphasis on understanding the difference between interpolation and extrapolation. Encourage discussion about when it is or isn’t appropriate to extrapolate beyond the given data range. Use examples where extrapolation leads to unrealistic or impractical results, such as predicting negative values for height or mass, to highlight the limitations of mathematical models. Make cross-curricular links with science, such as exploring the relationship between the length of a spring and the force applied. While this relationship may appear linear within a certain range, it no longer holds once the spring is overstretched. This helps students appreciate that extrapolation relies on assumptions and reinforces the importance of applying mathematical models carefully and critically.

baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students revisit their Year 8 knowledge by calculating averages and the range from a small data set. Start by reviewing how to calculate the mean, median, mode and range. Draw students’ attention to the fact that the range measures the spread of the data and is not an average. Highlight the importance of considering outliers and their impact on the averages. Once students are confident in calculating averages and the range, introduce more complex problems, such as finding an unknown value in a data set when given the mean, median, mode or range, or combinations of these.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Spring_Higher_Interpret and represent data_2_Averages from an ungrouped frequency table
small_step_name: Averages from an ungrouped frequency table
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students practise calculating the mean, median and mode from ungrouped frequency tables. Students have already covered calculating the mean from a frequency table in Year 8, but this may be their first time calculating the mode and median. Begin by helping students interpret the table, identifying the values and their frequencies. For the mean, guide them to multiply each value by its frequency, total these products and divide by the overall number of data points. When finding the mode, prompt students to identify the most frequent value. For the median, guide students to explore the cumulative frequency and find the middle value either through a cumulative frequency column or an ordered list.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Spring_Higher_Interpret and represent data_3_Mean from a grouped frequency table
small_step_name: Mean from a grouped frequency table
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students estimate the mean from grouped frequency tables. This may have previously been covered in Year 8 as an extend step. Begin by reviewing how to calculate the mean from raw data to highlight the difference when working with grouped data. Emphasise that when data is grouped, individual values are unknown, so the mean can only be estimated. Explain that the midpoint of each interval is used as a representative value, assuming an even distribution within each group. Model the process step by step, showing how to identify midpoints, multiply them by their corresponding frequencies, sum these products, and divide by the total frequency to find an estimated mean.

baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students revisit their Year 8 learning on discrete, continuous, quantitative and qualitative data, and explore the distinction between primary and secondary data. Those following the support scheme may not have previously encountered these data types, so it’s important to model clear examples and discuss each one to build understanding. Ask students to find secondary data on a related topic, such as national statistics or published survey results. Encourage them to discuss the advantages and disadvantages of each data source: primary data is usually more relevant but takes longer to collect, while secondary data is quicker to obtain but may be less specific or reliable.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Spring_Higher_Interpret and represent data_7_Sampling
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students develop their understanding of data collection by exploring sampling, a method used to gather information from part of a population when it isn’t practical to survey everyone. Begin by defining the population as the entire group being studied, such as all students in a school, and a sample as a smaller group representing it. Introduce random sampling, where each individual has an equal chance of being selected, and systematic sampling, where selections are made at regular intervals. Once students are confident, explore stratified sampling, where the population is divided into groups (strata) and a proportional sample is taken from each. Encourage students to apply proportional reasoning to calculate sample sizes and discuss which method is most reliable in different situations. Emphasise the importance of avoiding bias when selecting samples.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Spring_Higher_Interpret and represent data_8_Capture and recapture
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students use proportional reasoning to estimate a population with the capture–recapture method. Using familiar examples, such as estimating the number of fish in a pond, helps make the idea relatable and emphasises why estimation is needed when counting every individual is impractical. Begin by discussing the key assumption that the proportion of marked individuals in the second sample reflects the proportion in the entire population. For instance, if 10 fish are marked initially and, in a second sample of 20 fish, 2 are marked, then 10 N = 2 20 . Have students solve to calculate N to see how the population estimate arises from proportional reasoning. Conclude by discussing when estimates may be unreliable, such as when marked fish don’t mix evenly, highlighting the importance of the method’s assumptions.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Spring_Higher_Non-calculator methods_4_Convert recurring decimals to fractions
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students convert recurring decimals to fractions. In this step, students will only work with decimals with a single repeating digit. Build understanding by scaling known equivalences, for example, dividing 0.3 = 1 3 by 3 to show that 0.1 = 1 9 , and hence generalise that 0.a = a 9 where a is an integer between 1 and 9. Dividing 0.1 by 10 can show how 0.01 = 1 90 Algebraic approaches can also be used. Introduce attributing a decimal to an unknown and multiplying this by powers of 10 until two numbers with the same sequence of digits after the decimal point can be subtracted to give an integer. Students should be able to identify fractions that convert to a recurring decimal as well as use short division to complete conversions.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Spring_Higher_Non-calculator methods_5_Convert more complex recurring decimals to fractions (E)
small_step_name: Convert more complex recurring decimals to fractions (E)
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students convert decimals with two or more repeating digits into fractions. Highlight that the first digit with a recurring dot marks the start of a repeating sequence, which extends to the next digit with a recurring dot and then repeats indefinitely. Initially, it may be useful to model finding consecutive powers of ten of a decimal, for example, x, 10x, 100x, 1000x and so on, highlighting when two numbers have the same sequence of digits after the decimal point and how these could be subtracted to then form an equation then a fraction. As students build confidence, they may develop more efficient ways to solve problems through pattern spotting. This can link to the non- algebraic approaches explored in the previous step.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Spring_Higher_Non-linear graphs_1_Quadratic graphs
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students plot and interpret quadratic graphs. This step builds on understanding from Key Stage 3, introducing equations with negative coefficients of x2 It may be helpful to provide additional practice in substituting values, especially negative numbers, into quadratic expressions. Ensure students have opportunities to practise substitution both with and without a calculator. Remind students that the points should be joined smoothly, not with straight-line segments, and highlight the importance of correctly shaping the curve around the turning point. small_step_name: Intercepts and roots of quadratic graphs

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Spring_Higher_Non-linear graphs_8_Equation of a circle
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students are introduced to the equation of a circle, focusing on circles centred at the origin. Emphasise that the radius represents the distance from the origin (0, 0) to any point on the circumference of the circle. Demonstrate to students how a right-angled triangle can be formed by drawing a line from the centre of the circle, the origin, to a given point (x, y) on the circumference. This establishes how the equation of a circle can be written as x2 + y2 = r2 Students should be able to calculate the length of the radius from a diagram as well as from a given equation, such as recognising that a circle with an equation x2 + y2 = 144 has a radius of 12.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Spring_Higher_Probability_3_List and count outcomes
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students work systematically to list all possible outcomes in a given situation. Start with simple examples, such as flipping a coin or rolling a dice, before progressing to more complex examples. Encourage students to explain how they know their list is complete and that no outcomes have been missed. Modelling a systematic approach can help students understand that the total number of arrangements equals the product of the number of choices for each part. Students also need to distinguish between listing outcomes with and without replacement, and understand contexts where repeats are not allowed, such as finding the total number of handshakes in a group if each pair shakes hands once.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Spring_Higher_Probability_4_Relative frequency
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students consolidate their understanding from Key Stage 3, to consider relative frequency as a form of experimental probability. Students should recognise that probability is often considered in theoretical terms, where predictions are made about events that have not yet happened, while relative frequency is based on data from experiments or past events. Comparing theoretical probability with relative frequency can strengthen students’ understanding. A key discussion point is the effect of the number of trials on accuracy. Students should see that as the number of trials increases, the relative frequency tends to approach the theoretical probability. Students will also estimate the expected number of outcomes of an event using the relative frequency.

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Spring_Higher_Probability_7_Independent events
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students revisit independent events, first introduced in Key Stage 3. Distinguishing between independent and dependent events can be a challenging concept, so it is important to spend time ensuring students can recognise the difference. Independent events are those where the occurrence of one event does not affect the probability of the other. Once confident in identifying independent events, students apply the multiplication rule, P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B), to calculate the probability of two or more independent events occurring. This can then be extended by using the rule to test whether two events are independent.

Reinforce that the first significant figure is the first non-zero digit, but that zeros are classed as significant when they serve as a placeholder within a number. small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Spring_Higher_Straight line graphs_6_Find the midpoint of a line segment
small_step_name: Find the midpoint of a line segment
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students build on their knowledge of coordinates to find the midpoint of a line segment. Students may have previously explored this in Year 8 as an extend step. Begin by encouraging students to find the midpoint of two numbers on a number line, before transferring this skill to working in two dimensions. Students will learn that the mean of the x- and y-coordinates from a pair of points will give the x- and y-coordinates of the midpoint. Begin by modelling examples with line segments presented on a grid before students progress to working abstractly with two coordinates. If appropriate, students could work out the coordinates of the start or end point of a line segment given the midpoint. Challenge students to solve more complex problems involving midpoints and 2-D shapes.

baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students revisit key angle facts from Key Stage 3, including angles around a point, angles on a straight line and vertically opposite angles. Begin by recapping these rules using clear diagrams, and asking reasoning questions such as “What is the same and what is different?”, to help students recognise when angles sum to 180° or 360°, and when angles are equal. Emphasise the importance of selecting the correct rule for each scenario, and provide examples that require more than one rule to be applied. Encourage the consistent use of three-letter notation for angles, and correct use of angle symbols throughout. Ask students to explain their reasoning when identifying relationships between angles. small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Foundation_Angles_2_Angles in a triangle
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students recap prior learning from Key Stage 3 that the angles in a triangle sum to 180°. Begin by revisiting different types of triangles, and discussing how their angle properties compare. Encourage students to describe what is the same and what is different between examples, such as comparing angles in an isosceles and an equilateral triangle. Ensure students are confident using three-letter notation when identifying and labelling angles. Provide examples where students apply more than one angle fact, such as when finding unknown angles in triangles within larger diagrams. Encourage them to explain how they identified which facts to use, and to check their reasoning by verifying that the angles total 180°. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may confuse properties of different types of triangles. • Students may believe that the sum of angles in a triangle is 360°. • Students may believe that the sum of angles in all polygons is 180°, rather than just in triangles. small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Foundation_Angles_3_Angles in a quadrilateral
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students recap prior learning that the interior angles of a quadrilateral sum to 360°. Begin by highlighting the connection to the sum of angles in a triangle, showing how any quadrilateral can be divided into two triangles and hence, the angles in a quadrilateral sum to 360°. Use a range of examples, including rectangles, parallelograms, trapezia, and kites, to reinforce that the total is always 360°. Encourage students to provide reasons alongside their answers, and to label angles accurately using three-letter notation. baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students develop their understanding of factors, multiples and prime numbers, building on their learning from Key Stage 3. Encourage systematic listing strategies, identifying factor pairs to ensure that students list all the factors of a given number. Include square numbers, so that students are aware that the numbers in a factor pair may not always be different. Use counters to make the difference between factors and multiples explicit. Model factors as the way a number can be split into equal groups with no remainder, and multiples as repeated equal groups, linking multiples to times-table facts. Using the same number, such as 12, can help highlight the contrast. Use counters to reinforce that a prime number has exactly two distinct factors, 1 and itself, and remind students that 1 is not prime. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may think 1 is a prime number. • Students may confuse factors and multiples, listing multiples as factors or vice versa. • Students may stop factor lists too early and miss a factor pair. • Students may assume all odd numbers are prime. baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students build on their Key Stage 3 understanding of prime numbers and factors to write a number as a product of its prime factors. It can be helpful to begin with integers that have two or three prime factors before increasing complexity and introducing index notation. Encourage students to use a prime factor tree to organise information and identify prime factors. Ensure students understand that the product of the prime factors is equivalent to the original number. Emphasise that every integer greater than 1 has a unique prime factorisation, and that the order of the factors does not matter. As confidence increases, encourage students to make connections between the prime factor decomposition of related numbers. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may include non-prime factors in their final product. • Students may not work systematically, leading to missing or repeated factors. • Students may list prime factors, rather than writing them as a product. small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Foundation_Factors and powers_3_HCF and LCM
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students develop their learning from Key Stage 3 by finding the highest common factor (HCF) and lowest common multiple (LCM) of two or more numbers. Although both concepts are introduced in Key Stage 3, ensure the difference between them is made explicit and that students practise examples of each separately. Link HCF to sharing and grouping, and LCM to repeating patterns or cycles. It may be useful to use the same pair of numbers to find both the HCF and the LCM and compare how the methods and final answers differ. Once students are confident, they can progress to using Venn diagrams to calculate the HCF and LCM. When using Venn diagrams, model the process using prime factorisation and encourage students to check that their answer makes sense in context. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may confuse the HCF and LCM, especially when answering questions in context. • Students may assume the LCM of two numbers is always their product. • Students may place prime factors incorrectly in a Venn diagram, including duplicating factors, which leads to an incorrect HCF or LCM. Year 10 | Summer term | Block 4 – Factors, powers and surds | Step 3 Mathematical talk • What is a factor? • Explain what is meant by “highest common factor”. • What is a multiple? • Explain what is meant by “lowest common multiple”. • Is it possible to list all the multiples of a number? Why or why not? • How can prime factorisation help us find the HCF and LCM of two numbers more efficiently? • How can we decide whether a problem requires us to calculate the HCF or the LCM? • Can the HCF ever be greater than one of the numbers? Why or why not? F National Curriculum links • Use the concepts and vocabulary of prime numbers, factors (or divisors), multiples, common factors, common multiples, highest common factor, lowest common multiple, prime factorisation, including using product notation and the unique factorisation property (KS3)

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Foundation_Factors and powers_4_Square and cube numbers
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students develop fluency with square and cube numbers and their corresponding roots. Begin by modelling square numbers using concrete manipulatives, such as counters arranged in a square, before linking this to area models and the calculation of a number multiplied by itself. Model cube numbers using concrete volume representations, such as interlocking cubes, to demonstrate multiplying a number by itself twice, before moving to more abstract representations. Show how cube numbers can be generated from square numbers by multiplying by the original number. Encourage students to be familiar with the first 15 square numbers and at least the first five cube numbers to support later work with square and cube roots. Emphasise that square and cube roots are the inverse operations of squaring and cubing. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may confuse square and cube numbers. • Students may divide a number by 2 to calculate its square root or by 3 to calculate its cube root. • Students may believe that all square roots and cube roots are integers. Year 10 | Summer term | Block 4 – Factors, powers and surds | Step 4 Mathematical talk • What does it mean to “square” a number? • How is squaring different from multiplying by 2? • How can an area model help you visualise square numbers? • What is the difference between the square of a number and the square root of a number? • How can you use known square numbers to help identify square roots? • What is the same and what is different about squaring a number and cubing a number? • How do we calculate squares/cubes/roots on a calculator? • Why is the square root of 64 equal to 8 and not −8? • Are all square roots integer values? Explain your answer. F National Curriculum links • Use integer powers and associated real roots (square, cube and higher), recognise powers of 2, 3, 4, 5 and distinguish between exact representations of roots and their decimal approximations (KS3)

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Foundation_Factors and powers_5_Powers and roots
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students explore powers higher than cubes and their corresponding roots. Encourage students to rewrite powers as repeated multiplication, such as 24 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2, and remind them that finding a root is the inverse of raising a number to a power. Model using a calculator to evaluate powers and roots, including brackets with negative numbers. Use patterns to explore powers of negative numbers, focusing on how the sign changes with even and odd powers. Introduce zero powers through sequences such as 23, 22, 21, discussing why 20 = 1 Support estimation of square and higher roots by locating values between known powers and using this to check answers are sensible. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may confuse finding a root with division, dividing by the root index instead of finding the root itself, for example, calculating 32 ÷ 6 instead of finding the 6th root of 32 • Students may assume a negative base always gives a negative answer, rather than recognising that even powers give a positive result and odd powers give a negative result. • Students may misinterpret powers as multiplication by the exponent, rather than repeated multiplication, for example, interpreting 54 as 5 × 4 instead of 5 × 5 × 5 × 5 Year 10 | Summer term | Block 4 – Factors, powers and surds | Step 5 Mathematical talk • How can 46 be written as repeated multiplication? • What is the difference between 35 and 53? • Which value is greater, 34 or 43? Explain how you know. • What is the same and what is different between (–5)4 and –54? • What do you notice about the sign of (–2)n when n is even compared to when n is odd? Explain your answer. • What is the same and what is different about 64 and 64 6 ? • If 54 = 625, what is the 4th root of 625? How do you know? • Is the root of a number always smaller than the original number? Explain how you know. F National Curriculum links • Use integer powers and associated real roots (square, cube and higher), recognise powers of 2, 3, 4, 5 and distinguish between exact representations of roots and their decimal approximations (KS3)

baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this extend step, students develop their understanding of surds by expanding and simplifying single brackets involving surds. Begin with expanding single brackets and remind students that surds behave like algebraic terms and that the distributive law applies. Model expansion by multiplying each term inside the bracket by the term outside, using bar models or area models to support understanding. Once confident, students could be introduced to expanding and simplifying double brackets. Emphasise that only like surds can be combined. At this stage, avoid simplifying surds by factorising square factors, and instead focus on products that simplify directly to integers, such as 4 × 4 = 4 Misconceptions and common errors • Students may try to combine unlike surds after expansion, for example trying to simplify 2 + 3 • Students may assume a × a = a rather than a. • Students may multiply the integer and the surd incorrectly, for example writing 2 × 5 = 10 Year 10 | Summer term | Block 4 – Factors, powers and surds | Step 9 Mathematical talk • What is the same and what is different about expanding 3(x + 5) and 3( 2 + 5)? • What is the same and what is different about multiplying 3 × a and 3 × 5? • When we multiply two surds, what happens to the values inside the square root? • Explain why 2 × 2 = 4 can be simplified to an integer but 2 × 5 = 10 cannot. • Explain why 2 3 + 5 2 cannot be simplified. • What makes two surds “like surds”? Give an example. • Explain how you know when an expression with surds is fully simplified. small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Foundation_Graphs and diagrams_1_Pictograms
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students build on their prior learning of pictograms from Year 8. Begin by revisiting how discrete data is represented and how each symbol, or part of a symbol, corresponds to a value shown in the key. Highlight the importance of using the key carefully, both when constructing pictograms and when interpreting them. Once students are confident with this skill, support them in finishing partially completed pictograms by checking that the frequencies are shown correctly. Students should also practise interpreting pictograms by explaining what the data represents and making comparisons between categories where relevant. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may draw a pictogram without a key. • Students may choose a symbol for their key that makes it hard to represent part values. • Students may disregard the key and assume each symbol always represents one item. • Students may treat part symbols as whole symbols, leading to incorrect frequencies. Why or why not? small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Foundation_Graphs and diagrams_2_Line and bar charts
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students recap their Year 8 learning on constructing and interpreting vertical line charts and bar charts. Remind students that vertical line charts represent discrete data using lines drawn against various categories, with the height showing the frequency, while bar charts use rectangular bars to show the same information. Highlight that both charts use clearly labelled axes and consistent, equally spaced scales, with equal spacing between each line or bar. It can be helpful to compare a vertical line chart with a bar chart representing the same data to highlight the similarities in data presentation. As confidence develops, encourage students to compare frequencies and calculate the mode, range and mean from the charts. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may place numbers on the y-axis in unequal intervals resulting in a distorted scale. • Students may place vertical lines or bars at irregular gaps along the horizontal axis, rather than spacing them evenly. Year 10 | Summer term | Block 2 – Graphs and diagrams | Step 2 Mathematical talk • How do you know which axis shows the categories and which shows the frequency? • How can you describe the scale being used? • Do the lines or bars need an equal gap between them? Explain your answer. • How do you know what frequency each vertical line or bar represents? • What is the same and what is different about a vertical line chart and a bar chart? • If the scale goes up in 2s, where would you plot a frequency of 5? • How would this data look if it was shown in a different orientation? F National Curriculum links • Construct and interpret appropriate tables, charts, and diagrams, including frequency tables, bar charts, pie charts, and pictograms for categorical data, and vertical line (or bar) charts for ungrouped and grouped numerical data (KS3)

baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students recap their learning of drawing pie charts from Year 8. Remind students that a pie chart represents a total split into parts, with each category shown as a sector of a circle. The size of each sector is proportional to the frequency. Students can calculate the size of each sector using the formula, sector angle = frequency total × 360° to calculate the size of each sector. Model how to draw sectors accurately, using a protractor, highlighting the importance of labelling each sector clearly. As students increase in confidence, provide them with data in other formats such as percentages, fractions or data displayed in bar charts. small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Foundation_Graphs and diagrams_6_Time series graphs
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students recap their Year 7 learning on drawing and interpreting time series graphs. Remind them that these graphs show changes over time and require clearly labelled axes for accurate interpretation. Emphasise that time is always plotted on the horizontal axis and that equal intervals are essential. Encourage students to discuss upward or downward trends, along with periods of stability. Emphasise that while time series graphs highlight overall trends, short-term fluctuations may not always reflect the longer-term trend. Discuss with students how time series graphs with points joined by solid lines imply that it is possible to estimate information between data points, while points joined by dashed lines imply that the data between these points is not reliable. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may focus on specific points on a graph rather than the overall trends. • Students may assume that trends will always be consistent. • Students may use solid lines instead of dashed lines or vice versa. Year 10 | Summer term | Block 2 – Graphs and diagrams | Step 6 Mathematical talk • Does the time series graph have to start at zero? Explain your answer. • How can you show that your axis has not started from zero? • What does the overall trend of the graph show? • How can you describe the trend in this part of the graph? • Could there be a seasonal pattern? Explain your answer. • Is there a point that does not fit the general pattern? Why might that be? • Can the time series graph be used to estimate between data points? Explain your answer. • What similarities and what differences do you notice when comparing these two time series graphs? small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Foundation_Graphs and diagrams_7_Frequency polygons
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students draw and interpret frequency polygons. Begin by modelling how to construct a frequency polygon by identifying the midpoint of each class interval, plotting these points and joining them with straight lines. Highlight that the horizontal axis shows data from the class intervals as a continuous scale and the vertical axis shows the frequencies. Discuss with students why midpoints of the class intervals are used to plot the data on the horizontal axis and to describe what the shape of the frequency polygon shows, such as increases or decreases in the data. Model how to compare two frequency polygons on the same axes and explain how the overall shape helps students interpret and compare different distributions. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may plot the class boundaries rather than the midpoint. • Students may join the first and last points to form a polygon. • Students may draw bars instead of a polygon. • Students may incorrectly join the points using a curve instead of straight lines. Year 10 | Summer term | Block 2 – Graphs and diagrams | Step 7 Mathematical talk • What is the difference between a midpoint and an endpoint? • Given the boundaries of a class interval, how do you work out the midpoint? • Why do we plot the midpoint instead of the class boundaries? • How does the scale on a set of axes affect how a frequency polygon looks? • What does the steepest part of the polygon tell you about the data? • Does the line between two points represent actual data or an estimate? Explain how you know. F National Curriculum links • Interpret, analyse and compare the distributions of data sets from univariate empirical distributions through: appropriate graphical representation involving discrete, continuous and grouped data

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Foundation_Graphs and diagrams_8_Stem-and-leaf diagrams
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students draw and interpret stem-and-leaf diagrams. Begin by explaining that these diagrams organise numerical data, using the stem to show place value and the leaf to show the final digit, allowing all values to remain visible. Emphasise that including a clear key is essential so the data can be correctly interpreted. Model how to organise the data, select a suitable stem, and record each leaf clearly so digits align. Revisit how to calculate averages and the range by finding the difference between the greatest and smallest values in the set. Include examples with decimal values, such as 7|3 representing 7.3 As students develop confidence, introduce back-to-back stem- and-leaf diagrams to compare two data sets. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may write leaves out of order instead of listing them from smallest to largest. • Students may forget to include a key, which can make it difficult to interpret the values represented. Year 10 | Summer term | Block 2 – Graphs and diagrams | Step 8 Mathematical talk • What does the stem represent in this diagram? How do you know? • Why do we list the leaves in ascending order rather than the order they were collected? • Why is a key important when interpreting the values from a stem-and-leaf diagram? • What is the smallest value and what is the largest? How do you know? • What does the length of each row suggest about the distribution of values? • How would this diagram change if the data included decimals? • When might a back-to-back stem-and-leaf diagram be useful? small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Foundation_Vectors_3_Translate by a vector
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students explore vectors that are parallel to each other. Introduce students to the concept of a scalar, emphasising that it is the value by which a vector is multiplied. Students should recognise that when one vector is a scalar multiple of another, the two vectors are parallel. Begin by using diagrams to represent different vectors, for example by comparing a and 2a on a grid, highlighting that both are parallel and that 2a is twice the magnitude of a. This can then be used to build towards multiplying column vectors by a scalar. Emphasise that both the horizontal and vertical components of a column vector are multiplied by the scalar. Students should also have opportunities to explore the effect of multiplying vectors by negative scalars; for example, multiplying by –1 reverses the direction of a vector. baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students recap their learning of angles in triangles and quadrilaterals from Key Stage 3. small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Angles_3_Exterior angles of a polygon
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students recap their prior learning of interior and exterior angles from Key Stage 3. Remind them that the sum of the exterior angles of any polygon is 360° and use this to calculate individual exterior angles in regular polygons by dividing 360° by the number of sides. Highlight that interior and exterior angles sum to 180°, and use this to calculate unknown exterior angles given an interior angle. Students can then extend this knowledge to find the number of sides of a regular polygon when either the interior or exterior angle is known. Encourage students to clearly label diagrams to support reasoning, and to help identify when sides or angles are equal. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may believe that the exterior and interior angles sum to 360°. • Students may believe that the sum of exterior angles depends on the number of sides the polygon has. • Students may assume that some equal angles always mean the polygon is regular, without checking that all sides are also equal in length.
