small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Factors and powers_1_Prime factorisation, HCF and LCM
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students recap finding the highest common factor (HCF), lowest common multiple (LCM), and writing numbers as a product of prime factors from Key Stage 3. Use practical contexts to reinforce when HCF or LCM is needed, and model listing with small numbers to show why it becomes inefficient for greater values. Revisit prime factorisation using factor trees, emphasising that every integer greater than 1 has a unique prime factorisation. Use Venn diagrams to organise information, highlighting that the HCF is the product of the common factors, while the LCM is the product of all factors within the diagram. Link back to listing to show both methods give the same result. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may include non-prime factors in their final product. • Students may confuse factors and multiples, particularly when using listing methods. • Students may rely on listing methods for large numbers, leading to inefficiency and increased likelihood of error. • Students may multiply all prime factors when finding the HCF, rather than only those common to all numbers. small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Factors and powers_2_Powers, roots and negative indices
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students recap evaluating powers and roots, both mentally and using a calculator. Reinforce that a root is the inverse of a power, and ensure students can use calculator functions for powers and roots greater than 3. Support estimation by identifying the two integers a root lies between. Emphasise that a negative index does not make the value negative but instead indicates a reciprocal. Demonstrate this using a decreasing pattern, for example 22 = 4, 21 = 2, 20 = 1 and 2–1 = 1 2. Encourage students to generalise this to show that for any non-zero value of a, a–n = 1 an . Model converting negative indices into fractions with positive indices using numerical and algebraic examples, extending to bases with coefficients as confidence develops. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may assume that a negative index results in a negative answer, for example 3–2 = –9 • Students may multiply the base by the index instead of using a reciprocal, for example 2–3 = –6 • Students may misuse calculator functions for powers and roots, leading to incorrect evaluations. baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students explore fractional indices. Some students may have previously covered this as an extend step in Year 8. Ensure students are fluent with square roots, cube roots and higher roots before introducing fractional indices using numerical bases. Develop understanding by reasoning from index laws, for example 9 1 2 × 9 1 2 = 91, and link this to 9 = 3 since 3 × 3 = 9. Use this to generalise that the denominator of a fractional index indicates the root. small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Factors and powers_4_Four operations with surds
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students work with all four operations involving surds. The focus is on adding/subtracting like surds and multiplying/dividing surds by surds/integers. At this stage, surds do not need to be simplified beyond an integer result. For example, 3 × 5 can remain as 15, while 4 × 4 simplifies to 4. This keeps the focus on structure rather than technique, with further surd simplification developed in the next step. When adding and subtracting, emphasise that only like surds can be combined, just as only like algebraic terms can be collected, for example, 3 2 + 5 2 = 8 2 but 2 + 3 cannot be simplified further. When multiplying, model that a × b æ ab and that multiplying by an integer scales the surd, for example a × b = a b. If students are secure, you may choose to combine this step with simplifying surds further. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may try to add or subtract surds with different bases, for example 2 + 3 • Students may multiply integers and surds incorrectly, for example writing 2 × 5 = 10 • Students may not recognise when the product of surds simplifies to an integer, such as 4 × 4 = 4 Year 10 | Summer term | Block 4 – Factors, powers and surds | Step 4 Mathematical talk • Are surds rational or irrational? • When we multiply/divide two surds, what happens to the numbers inside the square roots? • Explain why 4 × 4 is equivalent to 4 • Is a + a equivalent to 2a ? small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Factors and powers_7_Rationalise the denominator
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students rationalise denominators that contain a single surd, building on their understanding of surds and rational numbers. Model the process by multiplying the numerator and denominator by the same surd so that the denominator becomes a rational number. For example, when the denominator is 2, multiply both the numerator and denominator by 2 so the denominator becomes 2. Emphasise that the value of the fraction does not change, only its form. Remind students to simplify the resulting fraction fully, including simplifying surds by considering square factors where possible. Keep the focus on single-term denominators such as 3 or 3 5. Rationalising denominators containing binomials will be covered later in the block. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may multiply only the denominator by the surd instead of multiplying both the numerator and denominator. • Students may think the value of the fraction changes when rationalising the denominator, rather than staying equivalent. • Students may not simplify fully after rationalising, including simplifying any surds or cancelling common factors. small_step_name: Rationalise the denominator with more complex denominators (E)
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this extend step, students will rationalise denominators with binomial expressions e.g. 1 + 5 2 Draw attention to the structure (a + b)(a – b), and highlight that this is a difference of two squares, simplifying to a2 – b, where the result will be an integer. small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Graphs and diagrams_10_Compare distributions using box plots (E)
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students learn how to compare distributions using box plots. Remind students that a box plot summarises a data set using the minimum, lower quartile, median, upper quartile and maximum values, allowing two or more distributions to be compared quickly on the same scale. Emphasise that comparisons should focus on a measure of average (median) and spread (range or interquartile range). Highlight that the relative positions of the medians can be used to decide which data set has the higher typical value. Encourage students to compare lengths of the boxes to judge differences in the interquartile ranges and discuss which data set shows greater consistency. Highlight the importance of using the same continuous scale so that comparisons are valid. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may draw incorrect conclusions, for example interpreting a larger range as an average or vice versa. • Students may incorrectly interpret the interquartile range or range, for example thinking a larger interquartile range is ‘better’. Year 10 | Summer term | Block 2 – Graphs and diagrams | Step 10 Mathematical talk • How do the positions of the medians help you compare trends in data sets? • Why is analysing the medians alone not enough to compare two data sets? • Which distribution shows a greater spread of data? How do you know? • How do the interquartile ranges compare? • What does a smaller interquartile range reveal about the spread of the middle half of the data? • How can you tell which data set is more consistent? • What do the “whiskers” tell you about the extremes in each data set? • What is the difference between the range and the interquartile range? Which of these measures might be affected by an outlier? H National Curriculum links • Interpret, analyse and compare the distributions of data sets from univariate empirical distributions through: appropriate graphical representation involving discrete, continuous and grouped data, {including box plots} E

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Graphs and diagrams_1_Pie charts
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students recap their learning from Year 8 on drawing and interpreting pie charts. Remind students that a pie chart represents a whole split into parts, with each sector showing a fraction of the total and all sectors summing to 360°. Make clear links between proportions, fractions and angles to show how they describe the same information. Emphasise the accurate use of a protractor when constructing sectors and highlight the importance of clear labelling. Introduce data given as percentages, fractions or bar charts for conversion into a pie chart. Encourage students to interpret pie charts by identifying key categories and, when comparing two charts, recognising that without totals only proportions can be compared. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may use the frequency as the angle size instead of working out the angle. • Students may not label the sectors. • When comparing two pie charts, students may assume equal sectors in different pie charts always represent the same frequency. small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Graphs and diagrams_2_Time series graphs
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students recap their Year 7 learning on drawing and interpreting time series graphs. Remind them that these graphs show changes over time and require clearly labelled axes for accurate interpretation. Emphasise that time is always plotted on the horizontal axis and that equal intervals are essential. Encourage students to discuss upward or downward trends, along with periods of stability. Emphasise that while time series graphs highlight overall trends, short-term fluctuations may not always reflect the longer-term trend. Discuss with students how time series graphs with points joined by solid lines imply that it is possible to estimate information between data points, while points joined by dashed lines imply that the data between these points is not reliable. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may focus on specific points on a graph rather than the overall trends. • Students may assume that trends will always be consistent. • Students may use solid lines instead of dashed lines or vice versa. Year 10 | Summer term | Block 2 – Graphs and diagrams | Step 2 Mathematical talk • Does the time series graph have to start at zero? Explain your answer. • How can you show that your axis has not started from zero? • What does the overall trend of the graph show? • How can you describe the trend in this part of the graph? • Could there be a seasonal pattern? Explain your answer. • Is there a point that does not fit the general pattern? Why might that be? • Can the time series graph be used to estimate between data points? Explain your answer. • What similarities and what differences do you notice when comparing these two time series graphs? H National Curriculum links • Interpret and construct tables and line graphs for time series data

small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Graphs and diagrams_3_Frequency polygons
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students draw and interpret frequency polygons. Begin by modelling how to construct a frequency polygon by identifying the midpoint of each class interval, plotting these points and joining them with straight lines. Highlight that the horizontal axis shows data from the class intervals as a continuous scale and the vertical axis shows the frequencies. Discuss with students why midpoints of the class intervals are used to plot the data on the horizontal axis and to describe what the shape of the frequency polygon shows, such as increases or decreases in the data. Model how to compare two frequency polygons on the same axes and explain how the overall shape helps students interpret and compare different distributions. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may plot the class boundaries rather than the midpoint. • Students may join the first and last points to form a polygon. • Students may draw bars instead of a polygon. • Students may incorrectly join the points using a curve instead of straight lines. Year 10 | Summer term | Block 2 – Graphs and diagrams | Step 3 Mathematical talk • What is the difference between a midpoint and an endpoint? • Given the boundaries of a class interval, how do you work out the midpoint? • Why do we plot the midpoint instead of the class boundaries? • How does the scale on a set of axes affect how a frequency polygon looks? • What does the steepest part of the polygon tell you about the data? • Does the line between two points represent actual data or an estimate? Explain how you know. small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Graphs and diagrams_4_Stem-and-leaf diagrams
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students draw and interpret stem-and-leaf diagrams. Begin by explaining that these diagrams organise numerical data, using the stem to show place value and the leaf to show the final digit, allowing all values to remain visible. Emphasise that including a clear key is essential so the data can be correctly interpreted. Model how to organise the data, select a suitable stem, and record each leaf clearly so digits align. Revisit how to calculate averages and the range by finding the difference between the greatest and smallest values in the set. Include examples with decimal values, such as 7|3 representing 7.3 As students develop confidence, introduce back-to-back stem- and-leaf diagrams to compare two data sets. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may write leaves out of order instead of listing them from smallest to largest. • Students may forget to include a key, which can make it difficult to interpret the values represented. Year 10 | Summer term | Block 2 – Graphs and diagrams | Step 4 Mathematical talk • What does the stem represent in this diagram? How do you know? • Why do we list the leaves in ascending order rather than the order they were collected? • Why is a key important when interpreting the values from a stem-and-leaf diagram? • What is the smallest value and what is the largest? How do you know? • What does the length of each row suggest about the distribution of values? • How would this diagram change if the data included decimals? • When might a back-to-back stem-and-leaf diagram be useful? Recap that histograms show continuous data and that the area of each bar represents frequency. baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students explore how cumulative frequency diagrams are constructed from grouped data. small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Graphs and diagrams_8_Interpret cumulative frequency diagrams
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students develop their understanding of cumulative frequency diagrams by interpreting the data shown. Remind students that each plotted point represents a cumulative total. Guide students to identify an estimate for the median and lower and upper quartiles by finding 25%, 50% and 75% of the total frequency and locating these values on the curve. small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Vectors_3_Vectors multiplied by a scalar
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students explore vectors that are parallel to each other. Introduce students to the concept of a scalar, emphasising that it is the value by which a vector is multiplied. Students should recognise that when one vector is a scalar multiple of another, the two vectors are parallel. Begin by using diagrams to represent different vectors, for example by comparing a and 2a on a grid, highlighting that both are parallel and that 2a is twice the magnitude of a. Students should also have opportunities to explore the effect of multiplying vectors by negative scalars; for example, multiplying by –1 reverses the direction of a vector. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may make arithmetic errors, particularly when using negative numbers. • Students may struggle to represent vector subtraction problems as diagrams. • Students may neglect one of the values in a column vector when multiplying by a scalar. small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Vectors_6_Vector journeys in shapes
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students explore different ways to express vector journeys, combining successive movements as vector calculations. This step builds the foundations needed for students to form geometric proofs later. Students learn to express a route such as AB + BC + CD = AD showing that multiple vectors can represent a single resultant vector. Students then move to simplifying expressions or comparing routes algebraically, for example, by writing a + b + 2a – b as 3a. Draw students’ attention to the fact that different routes can have the same resultant vector. Highlight the effect of reversing the direction of a vector, for example, if MN = a – 2b then NM = –a + 2b. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may neglect the direction of arrows on a vector diagram, such as using the vector a rather than –a. • Students may struggle to find a route using known vectors. • Students may make arithmetic errors, particularly with negative terms. Year 10 | Summer term | Block 3 – Vectors | Step 6 Mathematical talk • How can we describe a journey from one vertex to another using vectors? • How can we show that AB + BC = AC on a diagram? • How is XY related to YX ? • Why does taking different routes around a shape sometimes give the same resultant vector? • Can the same journey be described using a different combination of vectors? • If EF = a and FG = b, how could we describe EG in terms of a and b? • Why is it important to use consistent notation when writing vector journeys? small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Vectors_7_Vectors in quadrilaterals
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students apply their knowledge of vector journeys while considering the properties of quadrilaterals such as rectangles, parallelograms, and trapezia. Encourage students to discuss the properties of different quadrilaterals, for example, parallelograms have two pairs of parallel sides. Highlight that this means a parallelogram has two pairs of identical vectors. Draw students’ attention to the direction of arrows on diagrams and how this can affect the result of a vector journey and the accurate evaluation of vector addition or subtraction. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may neglect the direction of arrows on a vector diagram, such as using the vector a rather than –a. • Students may not recognise properties leading to vectors which aren’t labelled on diagrams. small_step_id: Year 10_14-15_Summer_Higher_Vectors_8_Parallel vectors
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students explore parallel vectors, recognising that vectors are parallel when one is a scalar multiple of the other. Students may have some understanding of this concept from earlier steps in this block. Highlight that parallel vectors have the same (or opposite) direction but may differ in magnitude. Support strategies for proving that column vectors are parallel by using vectors represented on grids to emphasise the link between vectors and scalars. After this, model how to prove that algebraic vectors are parallel through factorisation. Once students are confident, move on to more complex problems where they may need to consider vector journeys to compare two vectors. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may think vectors are parallel if they have the same magnitude. • Students may not recognise parallel vectors involving negative scalars. For example, writing 6 2 -   as –2 × -3 1   to show 6 2 -   and -3 1   are parallel. • Students may find it difficult to write algebraic expressions for vectors that represent movement in the opposite direction. Year 10 | Summer term | Block 3 – Vectors | Step 8 Mathematical talk • What does it mean for two vectors to be parallel? • How can we tell if one column vector is a multiple of another? • Can two vectors be parallel but point in opposite directions? Explain how you know. • How can we tell if two vectors in terms of a and b are parallel? • What happens to a vector when it is multiplied by a negative scalar? • Why do parallel vectors not have to be equal in length? • Are two vectors that are equal in magnitude always parallel? Why or why not? small_step_id: Year 11_15-16_Autumn_Foundation_Area and volume_10_Convert metric units of area (E)
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students convert metric units of area. This may have been previously explored in the extend step in Year 9. Begin by exploring a square with a side length of 1 cm and comparing it to a square with a side length of 10 mm, highlighting that both lengths are equivalent. This leads to the key insight that 1 cm² is equal to 100 mm2 A similar approach can be used to compare other metric units, such as converting between m2 and cm2. Encourage students to recognise that the area scale factor is the square of the linear scale factor. Once students are confident, they can progress to converting between units in a single calculation for example, converting 3 cm2 to mm2

small_step_id: Year 11_15-16_Autumn_Foundation_Area and volume_1_Isometric drawings
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students draw and interpret 3-D shapes on isometric paper. Students may be familiar with isometric paper when exploring volumes in cuboids in Key Stage 2. Ensure students know that adjacent dots on isometric paper are equidistant. Start by having students draw cubes and cuboids isometrically made from centimetre cubes, before drawing cubes and cuboids with labelled integer dimensions. Encourage students to start drawing the shape from its base towards the bottom of the isometric paper, so that they do not run out of room. When ready, have students practise drawing and interpreting triangular prisms isometrically. Having 3-D shapes available will help students to understand how the shape is represented using the isometric paper. Volume of cubes, cuboids and triangular prisms can be interleaved in this step.

baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students will draw accurate and scaled plans as well as front and side elevations of 3-D shapes. small_step_id: Year 11_15-16_Autumn_Foundation_Area and volume_3_Volume of a cylinder
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students will build on prior learning from Year 10, combining their understanding of the area of a circle and the volume of prisms. Highlight that, although cylinders are not prisms, the volume of a cylinder is calculated in a similar way by multiplying the area of the constant cross-section by the length or height. Allow students the opportunity to practise giving answers exactly in terms of pi (π) and to various degrees of accuracy, for example, rounded to 1 decimal place. If appropriate, students could solve problems involving the volume of a cylinder, for example calculating an unknown length within the cylinder.

small_step_id: Year 11_15-16_Autumn_Foundation_Area and volume_4_Volume of a sphere
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students use the formula to calculate the volume of a sphere. Tell students that the formula to work out the volume of a sphere with radius r is 4 3 πr3, and model how to input relevant calculations into a calculator, for example 4 3 × π × 53, to work out the volume of a sphere with a radius of 5 cm. As with other formulae involving pi (π), students should have the opportunity to provide exact answers in terms of pi (π), as well as giving approximate answers to varying degrees of accuracy. When students are comfortable with finding the volume of a sphere, they could begin to investigate the volume of hemispheres and compound shapes.

small_step_id: Year 11_15-16_Autumn_Foundation_Area and volume_5_Volume of cones and pyramids
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students calculate the volume of cones and pyramids. Students may not have covered this before, as this is an extend step in Year 9. When introducing the volume of a cone, it may be useful to draw out similarities with the formula for the volume of a cylinder. That is, the volume of a cone is 1 3 of the volume of a cylinder with the same height and radius. Then further similarity may be shown between the formulae for cones and pyramids. For example, the volume of both can be calculated with 1 3 × area of base × height. If appropriate, students could form and solve equations involving volumes, such as calculating the length of a radius when given the height and volume of a cone.

small_step_id: Year 11_15-16_Autumn_Foundation_Area and volume_6_Surface area of a sphere
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students will calculate the surface area of a sphere using the formula. Remind students that the surface area is the area that covers the outside of a 3-D shape, and introduce them to the formula Area = 4πr2. small_step_id: Year 11_15-16_Autumn_Foundation_Set notation and Venn diagrams_2_Set notation
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students consolidate and build on learning from Year 9, identifying and representing sets using set notation. This content is new for students who have exclusively followed the support curriculum, so reviewing the Year 9 main curriculum may help reinforce understanding. Students need to be able to identify elements of a set given a description and describe a set given the elements. Having already explored the structure of a Venn diagram, students will also identify and interpret the part that represents the intersection or union of two or more sets, as well as the complement of a set. Students may need reminding that set A includes the intersection, A ∩ B, in a standard Venn diagram. Using colour or shading to highlight these areas is useful to support students’ understanding.

small_step_id: Year 11_15-16_Autumn_Foundation_Set notation and Venn diagrams_3_Probabilities from Venn diagrams
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students build on their understanding of Venn diagrams and set notation to work out probabilities. Remind students how to interpret different regions of a Venn diagram. Start with completed Venn diagrams with “countable” elements, for example, classifying shapes as “blue shapes” or “squares”. Model how to find the probability of choosing, for example, a blue square at random, by writing the number of blue squares as a fraction of the total number of shapes. Ensure that students practise writing probabilities of each region in the Venn diagram, to build understanding. As confidence develops, move onto Venn diagrams with numerical data, interleaving the use of set notation where appropriate.

small_step_id: Year 11_15-16_Autumn_Foundation_Similarity and congruence_1_Identify similar shapes
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students will revisit their understanding of similar shapes from Key Stage 3. Students will build on their knowledge of enlargement to identify similar shapes. Begin by encouraging students to calculate the scale factor of enlargement for each corresponding length and highlight that if the scale factor is the same, the shapes must be similar. Remind students that angles in corresponding positions in similar shapes are equal. Once students are confident in identifying similar shapes using scale factors, they can begin to incorporate ratios to determine if shapes are similar.

small_step_id: Year 11_15-16_Autumn_Foundation_Similarity and congruence_2_Find unknown lengths and angles in similar shapes
small_step_name: Find unknown lengths and angles in similar shapes
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students calculate unknown angles and lengths in similar shapes, building on learning from Key Stage 3. Ensure students identify corresponding sides correctly, drawing attention to examples where the shapes have different orientations. Model strategies to calculate the scale factor of enlargement between the shapes, ensuring students can work with both integer and fractional scale factors, for example the scale factor from shape A to B and shape B to A. Students should be aware that corresponding angles in similar shapes are equal. Encourage the use of geometric notation when labelling side lengths and angles.

small_step_id: Year 11_15-16_Autumn_Foundation_Similarity and congruence_3_Identify similar triangles
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students apply their knowledge of angle facts to show that a pair of triangles are similar. Remind students of facts involving angles that are vertically opposite, angles that form a straight line and angles that exist within pairs of parallel lines. Ensure students see a variety of examples including triangles that share a vertex as well triangles embedded within each other, sharing a common angle. Support students to identify the corresponding vertices of two similar triangles. Highlight that if all three angles in one triangle are the same as the angles in another, then the triangles are similar. If necessary, it may be appropriate to encourage students to draw the triangles separately and in the same orientation before working out unknown lengths and angles. Students should also recognise that using side ratios is an equally valid method of establishing similarity.

small_step_id: Year 11_15-16_Autumn_Foundation_Similarity and congruence_4_Solve problems with similar shapes
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students consolidate and extend their understanding of similar shapes. Begin with a mixture of questions from previous steps where students calculate scale factors between similar shapes, determining if two shapes are similar and calculating unknown lengths and angles. Once students are confident, include problems involving similar triangles. Demonstrate strategies to help visualise the problem, such as drawing any shapes with a common vertex or angle as two separate shapes in the same orientation. Students should be encouraged to discuss their approaches and reasoning when solving the problems. It may be appropriate to interleave other topic areas such as Pythagoras’ theorem or trigonometry.

small_step_id: Year 11_15-16_Autumn_Foundation_Similarity and congruence_5_Prove a pair of triangles are similar (E)
small_step_name: Prove a pair of triangles are similar (E)
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this extend step, students explore general examples of similar triangles and use formal proofs to justify their similarity. They may need reminders about angle rules, such as those involving parallel lines, to help identify equal angles within a shape. Emphasise the importance of using correct geometric notation when labelling angles and lengths in their proofs. Demonstrate how to structure explanations clearly and precisely to strengthen their justifications. Reinforce that triangles are similar if all corresponding angles are equal or if their corresponding side lengths are proportional. Where appropriate, challenge students to apply Pythagoras’ theorem within similar right-angled triangles.

baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students explore the differences between similarity and congruence. When introducing the volume of a cone, it may be useful to draw out similarities with the formula for the volume of a cylinder. baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students explore the theorem that a perpendicular line segment from the centre of a circle to a chord, bisects the chord. Ensure students are confident in their understanding of what a chord is. Emphasise the fact that when a radius bisects a chord, the angle between the radius and the chord is always 90°. The use of dynamic geometry software allows students to manipulate the position of the chord and to observe that the perpendicular relationship remains consistent. If appropriate, relate this topic to construction and loci, modelling that a perpendicular bisector of a chord must pass through the centre of a circle, and doing this twice on separate chords in turn locates the centre of the circle.

small_step_id: Year 11_15-16_Autumn_Higher_Circle theorems_7_Circle theorem (angle between radius and tangent)
small_step_name: Circle theorem (angle between radius and tangent)
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students explore the theorem that the angle between a radius and tangent of a circle, that meet at the same point on the circumference, is 90°. Ensure students understand that a tangent is a line that touches the circumference of the circle at only one point. Dynamic geometry software can help students to visualise how this remains true as the tangent moves or the circle’s size changes. Encourage students to annotate diagrams with angles, for example, labelling known right angles. As students’ understanding develops, explore problems where other right-angled related topics are present, for example, using Pythagoras’ theorem to find unknown lengths of line segments.

small_step_id: Year 11_15-16_Autumn_Higher_Circle theorems_8_Circle theorem (two tangents from a point)
small_step_name: Circle theorem (two tangents from a point)
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students explore the theorem that two tangents from a single external point to the circle are equal in length. Allow students to observe the lengths of the tangents in many orientations, using dynamic geometry software to move the external point around outside the circle, as well as towards and further away from the circumference. Emphasise that these tangents are of equal length and therefore form an isosceles triangle when a chord connects the tangents’ points of contact with the circumference. Additionally, drawing radii from the circle’s centre to the tangents, and a line segment to connect the external point to the centre, forms two congruent right-angled triangles. Encourage students to annotate diagrams with known angles and lengths, marking right angles where the radius meets the tangent and identifying equal tangent lengths. As their understanding develops, explore problems where they apply this relationship in other areas of maths, such as pairs of congruent triangles and properties of kites.

small_step_id: Year 11_15-16_Autumn_Higher_Circle theorems_9_Circle theorem (alternate segment theorem) (E)
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this extend step, students explore the alternate segment theorem, which states that the angle between a tangent and a chord at the point of contact is equal to the angle in the alternate segment. Students must understand that a segment is the region enclosed by a chord and its arc, with the larger area as the major segment and the smaller as the minor segment. Highlight the angle between the tangent and chord meeting on the circumference and the angle in the alternate segment. Measure both angles to emphasise their equality. Explore the relationship further by adjusting the chord or tangent using dynamic geometry software. As understanding develops, provide problems to apply this theorem with other circle theorems.

small_step_id: Year 11_15-16_Autumn_Higher_Ratio and proportion_1_Solve problems with ratio
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students will revisit problems involving ratio covered in Year 10. Provide opportunities for students to share amounts in a ratio when given either a total, a part, or a difference. Bar models can help students to identify key differences between problems and to establish a suitable strategy to solve them, rather than relying on a procedural method, such as dividing an amount by the sum of the parts in a given ratio. Students should also explore links between fractions and ratios. Note that “combine a set of ratios” and “link ratio and algebra” are both Extend steps in Year 10 and may not have been covered previously. Time could be given to each of these steps if appropriate.

small_step_id: Year 11_15-16_Autumn_Higher_Ratio and proportion_2_Best buy problems
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students will solve financial problems, building on prior learning from Key Stage 3. Provide students opportunities to explore different strategies to compare items and cost, for example, scaling to compare the same amount of each item or working out the unit cost of each item. It is important to discuss when different strategies may be more efficient than others. Students should also be able to solve problems with common everyday life special offers, for example, “20% off’” or “3 for 2” offers. The use of a calculator is recommended for this step to place more emphasis on strategies to solve problems rather than mental arithmetic.

small_step_id: Year 11_15-16_Autumn_Higher_Ratio and proportion_3_Conversion graphs
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students draw and interpret conversion graphs to complete approximate conversions. Explain to students that if a conversion graph forms a straight line passing through the origin, it represents a direct proportion. Encourage students to draw a line segment to the graph when reading a value from the axes. Students can also use the learning from the previous step to work out values that are not in the range of the data represented on a graph. For example, if a graph shows that 5 cm ≈ 2 inches, then 50 cm ≈ 20 inches. Unfamiliar contexts, such as converting metric units to imperial units, are useful to encourage students to use a graph for their conversions.

small_step_id: Year 11_15-16_Autumn_Higher_Ratio and proportion_5_Direct proportion equations
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students will use their understanding of direct proportion to form equations. Students will be introduced to the symbol ∝, which is used to denote when two variables are proportional. For example, y ∝ x means y is proportional to x, which implies direct proportion. Highlight that direct proportion equations are written in the form y = kx, where x and y are variables and k is the constant of proportionality. Encourage students to substitute known information into their formula to work out the constant of proportionality. They will then use this constant to work out different corresponding values of the variables. Students can also solve problems in context. For example, the cost, c, of pens is directly proportional to the number of pens, p.

small_step_id: Year 11_15-16_Autumn_Higher_Ratio and proportion_7_Inverse proportion
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students explore the relationship between quantities that are inversely proportional. Students should understand that if two quantities are inversely proportional, then when one amount increases, the other amount decreases at the same rate. Students’ attention should be drawn to the fact that the product of the two quantities is constant as the quantities vary. It may be useful to begin with a scenario involving one person, such as 1 person takes 4 hours to paint a fence, before moving on to more challenging problems. Encourage students to think about whether a task will take more or less time with more people. Throughout the step, discuss any assumptions that have been made, such as assuming every person works at the same rate.

Highlight to students that the terms “linear sequence” and “arithmetic sequence” are interchangeable. Students should have opportunities to use term-to-term rules to generate and describe sequences. Sequences with algebraic terms may be introduced, but keep in mind that this is specifically looked at in the next step. It is not necessary to consider nth term rules in this step, as this is covered later in the block.

small_step_id: Year 11_15-16_Autumn_Higher_Set notation and Venn diagrams_2_Venn diagrams
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students create and interpret Venn diagrams and work out probabilities from them. It is important for students to understand that the large rectangle around the circles represents all possible elements, denoted by the universal set, ξ. By understanding the structure of a Venn diagram, students will be able to sort and interpret information efficiently, investigating whether sets intersect or whether they are mutually exclusive. Emphasise the difference between questions such as “Who plays hockey?” compared with “Who plays only hockey”? Ensure that students practise writing probabilities of each region in the Venn diagram, and as confidence develops, move on to Venn diagrams with three circles.

small_step_id: Year 11_15-16_Autumn_Higher_Set notation and Venn diagrams_3_Solve problems with Venn diagrams
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students build on learning from previous steps in the block to solve problems with Venn diagrams. The problems appear in different forms, incorporating other topics such as solving equations and fractions of amounts. It may be worth investing time to read through questions as a class and explore useful strategies before students work on these independently. Goal-free problems are an excellent way to take the emphasis away from finding an answer, instead encouraging students to focus on what can be worked out and how. It may be beneficial to start with problems that are broken down into individual steps, before progressing to more complex problems. If appropriate, more advanced set notation such as P(A ∪ B)’ can be used.

small_step_id: Year 11_15-16_Autumn_Higher_Similarity and congruence_2_Identify similar triangles
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students apply their knowledge of angle facts to show that a pair of triangles are similar. Remind students of facts involving angles that are vertically opposite, angles that form a straight line and angles that exist within pairs of parallel lines. Ensure students see a variety of examples including triangles that share a vertex as well triangles embedded within each other, sharing a common angle. Support students to identify the corresponding vertices of two similar triangles. Highlight that if all three angles in one triangle are the same as the angles in another, then the triangles are similar. If necessary, it may be appropriate to encourage students to draw the triangles separately and in the same orientation before working out unknown lengths and angles. Students should also recognise that using side ratios is an equally valid method of establishing similarity.

small_step_id: Year 11_15-16_Autumn_Higher_Standard form_1_Numbers in standard form
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students recap and consolidate their knowledge of standard form from Key Stage 3. They will revisit conversion to and from standard form, as well as comparing and ordering numbers in standard form. Students may need reminding of the correct form A × 10n, where 1 ≤ A < 10 and n is an integer. Students need to able to recognise when a number is or is not in standard form; using non-examples such as 0.6 × 10–5 is encouraged. Using numbers in context, such as diameters of planets, helps to highlight why standard form is an efficient way to write large numbers. This step also includes opportunities to adjust a number to standard form.

small_step_name: Four operations with numbers in standard form
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students perform the four operations on numbers written in standard form. Mental, written and calculator methods should all be explored. Recapping index laws may be helpful before multiplying and dividing numbers written in standard form. For adding and subtracting, students should begin with calculations where the power of 10 is the same in each number before progressing to those where they differ. Encourage students to discuss whether they prefer to convert to ordinary numbers before adding or subtracting, or whether they are comfortable using their knowledge of place value. Throughout this step, ensure students adjust answers to correct standard form where needed. Calculations involving a combination of operations will be covered in the next step.

small_step_id: Year 11_15-16_Spring_Foundation_Constructions and Loci_1_Use geometrical equipment
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students use protractors and compasses to construct and measure accurately. This step allows pupils to practise using geometrical equipment in preparation for accurately drawing polygons and completing constructions. Remind students how to measure angles correctly with a protractor, drawing attention to the two scales and explaining when each should be used. Provide opportunities for them to practise using a pair of compasses by drawing circles and arcs before progressing to circles with a specified radius or diameter. Demonstrate how to measure the required radius by aligning the compass points with a ruler to ensure accuracy. If possible, use a visualiser to model correct compass technique, emphasising the need to maintain the set distance on the compass while drawing.

small_step_id: Year 11_15-16_Spring_Foundation_Constructions and Loci_2_Accurately draw triangles
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students accurately draw triangles. Students accurately draw triangles when given two angles and a side length between them (ASA), two side lengths and an angle between them (SAS) or three side lengths (SSS). Begin by modelling how to accurately draw ASA and SAS triangles with a ruler and a protractor, before modelling how to use a pair of compasses to construct an SSS triangle. Highlight that students should keep any construction lines on a completed drawing. Encourage students to measure angles and/ or sides to check their drawings are accurate. Use of a visualiser is recommended when accurately drawing triangles.

small_step_id: Year 11_15-16_Spring_Foundation_Constructions and Loci_4_Construct an angle bisector
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students bisect an angle using a pair of compasses, a skill that will later be applied to solving loci problems within this block. Students may have encountered constructing angle bisectors in Year 9 Explain that bisecting an angle divides it into two equal parts. Use a visualiser to model the process of constructing an angle bisector with a pair of compasses. Once students are confident with bisecting a single angle, extend their understanding by asking them to bisect angles within polygons. Encourage them to check the accuracy of their constructions by measuring the resulting angles with a protractor. Later in the block, students will connect angle bisectors to the concept of a locus that is equidistant from two lines.

small_step_id: Year 11_15-16_Spring_Foundation_Constructions and Loci_5_Construct a perpendicular bisector
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students use a pair of compasses to construct the perpendicular bisector of a line segment, a skill they may have previously encountered in Year 9. This step provides an opportunity to revisit and practise the technique before applying it to loci problems. Explain that a perpendicular bisector meets a line at a 90° angle and divides it into two equal parts. Use a visualiser to demonstrate how to construct a perpendicular bisector accurately. Emphasise that the compass width should be set to more than half the length of the line segment so that the arcs intersect. Remind students that both arcs must be drawn with the same radius to ensure the line segment is bisected precisely.

small_step_name: Construct a perpendicular from or to a point
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students construct a perpendicular of a line passing through a specific point, which may have been previously covered in Year 9. Use a visualiser to model constructing intersections of a given line before drawing a perpendicular.

small_step_id: Year 11_15-16_Spring_Foundation_Constructions and Loci_7_Locus of distance from a point or a straight line
small_step_name: Locus of distance from a point or a straight line
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students learn that a locus is a set of points that share a common property, such as all points 4 cm from a given point. Emphasise that the locus of points a fixed distance from a point forms a circle and discuss how the wording of a question determines whether it refers to points inside, on, or outside the circle. For example, how points within the circle represent distances less than the given radius. Encourage students to explore and label these regions clearly. Students also investigate the locus of points a fixed distance from a line, and can extend this concept by constructing loci around other shapes, such as squares.

baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students build on prior learning from Year 10 to solve inequalities. Remind students of the differences between an equation and an inequality. small_step_id: Year 11_15-16_Spring_Foundation_Equations and formulae_5_Form and solve inequalities (E)
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students form and solve inequalities. Begin by encouraging students to form and solve simple 1- and 2- step inequalities before progressing to forming inequalities with unknowns on both sides. Highlight that if no unknown is specified within a question, any letter could be used to form an initial inequality. Ensure that students are also given opportunities to discuss solutions in context. For example, if n represents the number of people, then the minimum or maximum number of people should be an integer.

small_step_id: Year 11_15-16_Spring_Foundation_Equations and formulae_6_Form and solve more complex equations and inequalities (E)
small_step_name: Form and solve more complex equations and inequalities (E)
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this extend step, students solve equations and inequalities in different forms, such as equations involving fractions or compound inequalities. Support students when forming and solving compound inequalities by modelling how to combine two inequalities, for example writing 2x > 12 and 2x < 20 as 12 < 2x < 20 Provide opportunities for students to discuss when an inequality can be represented as a compound inequality due to the context. For example, if (x – 30)° represents the size of an angle that must be less than 50° this can be written as x – 30 < 50, so x < 80 However, since an angle cannot be 0° or negative, x must be greater than 30. Therefore, the complete inequality is 30 < x < 80

baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students revisit and consolidate using function machines with numerical inputs and outputs, before progressing to working with algebraic expressions in subsequent steps. small_step_id: Year 11_15-16_Spring_Foundation_Functions and graphs_3_Quadratic graphs
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students consolidate their understanding of quadratic graphs. Students will use completed tables to generate and plot coordinate pairs for quadratic functions. When plotting, model how to draw a smooth curve through the points rather than connecting them with straight lines. Progress to identifying turning points from graphs and reading or estimating roots. Begin with simple quadratic functions such as y = x² or y = x² + 1 and guide students to the solutions to a quadratic equation, for example x² – 5 = 0 being the points where the graph y = x² – 5 crosses the x-axis. Once students are confident, introduce the concept of plotting an additional straight line on a graph to estimate solutions to a new equation, for example, drawing the line y = 4 to solve x² + 3x + 2 = 4

small_step_id: Year 11_15-16_Spring_Foundation_Transformations_1_Enlargement (positive scale factor)
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students enlarge shapes using positive integer scale factors, building on their understanding of similarity. Start with enlargements on a grid and highlight that scale factors greater than 1 produce larger images. As students progress, introduce enlargements with a given centre of enlargement. Encourage students to count distances from the centre of enlargement to each vertex of the shape and multiply it by the scale factor to determine the corresponding vertices of the image. Provide practice using centres that are not at the origin. Students should also work out the scale factor of an enlargement, and identify the centre of enlargement by drawing ray lines through the corresponding vertices of the object and image. The point where the ray lines meet is the centre of enlargement. Encourage students to use a ruler for accuracy and extend lines beyond the image if necessary.

small_step_id: Year 11_15-16_Spring_Foundation_Transformations_6_Translation
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students recap their Year 9 learning of translations by translating shapes and describing translations using column vectors. Begin by describing column vectors in words, before applying the column vector to the concept of translation. Explain that students must specify the movement in both the horizontal and vertical directions to describe a translation fully, and remind them of the importance of the positive and negative signs in column vectors.

baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students learn to describe a series of transformations as a single transformation. Begin by having students perform two successive transformations, such as a rotation followed by a reflection, and ask them to compare the original and final shapes. Encourage them to look for a direct link between the start and end positions, identifying whether the combined effect is equivalent to a single transformation. Discuss common patterns, such as two successive reflections across parallel lines being equivalent to a translation, or two rotations around the same point combining into a single rotation. Stem sentences can be useful to support structured explanations. Encourage students to justify their reasoning and test their ideas by reversing transformations to check their conclusions.

small_step_id: Year 11_15-16_Spring_Higher_Angles bearings and trigonometry_1_Understand and represent bearings
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students are introduced to bearings as a specific type of angle, always measured clockwise from north and expressed using three figures. Use real-world contexts such as giving directions, map reading or aviation problems to illustrate the concept. Provide both examples and non-examples to deepen understanding. Highlight the wording “bearing of A from B”, as this can often cause confusion, and emphasise identifying the angle carefully with a range of start and end points. Discuss the convention that the north line is typically drawn vertically up the page, regardless of the actual direction of north. Throughout this step, make regular connections to angles within compass points.

small_step_id: Year 11_15-16_Spring_Higher_Angles bearings and trigonometry_2_Measure and read bearings
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students learn how to measure and read bearings in a variety of problem-solving contexts with a focus on interpreting diagrams and using protractors. Students may need to refer to the rules of bearings from the previous step throughout when practising this new skill. A visualiser is useful for modelling and to support students’ understanding.

baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students learn that a locus is a set of points that share a common property, such as all points 4 cm from a given point. Emphasise that the locus of points a fixed distance from a point forms a circle and discuss how the wording of a question determines whether it refers to points inside, on, or outside the circle. Students also investigate the locus of points a fixed distance from a line, and can extend this concept by constructing loci around other shapes, such as squares.

small_step_id: Year 11_15-16_Spring_Higher_Transformations_1_Enlargement (positive scale factor)
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students enlarge shapes using positive integer scale factors, building on their understanding of similarity. Start with enlargements on a grid and highlight that scale factors greater than 1 produce larger images. As students progress, introduce enlargements with a given centre of enlargement. Encourage students to count distances from the centre of enlargement to each vertex of the shape and multiply it by the scale factor to determine the corresponding vertices of the image. Provide practice using centres that are not at the origin. Students should also work out the scale factor of an enlargement, and identify the centre of enlargement by drawing ray lines through the corresponding vertices of the object and image. The point where the ray lines meet is the centre of enlargement. Encourage students to use a ruler for accuracy and extend lines beyond the image if necessary.

small_step_id: Year 11_15-16_Spring_Higher_Transformations_9_Invariant points (E)
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students develop their understanding of invariant points and lines by observing which parts of a shape remain unchanged during different transformations. Begin by demonstrating a reflection where the shape touches the mirror line, and ask students to identify points that have not moved. Highlight to students that points on the mirror line are invariant. Repeat with other transformations, highlighting that invariant points occur in rotations only when the centre lies on a vertex or edge of the shape. Similarly, in enlargements, this occurs only when the centre of enlargement is on the shape itself. When discussing enlargements, note special cases such as a scale factor of 1, where all points are invariant. Emphasise that translations have no invariant points, as every point moves the same distance and direction, unless the shape remains unchanged.

small_step_id: Year 1_5-6_Autumn__Addition and subtraction within 10_2_Part-whole model
baseline_ss_wr_desc: Now that children have explored parts and wholes, in this small step they are introduced to the part-whole model. This is sometimes referred to as a “cherry model”. The main teaching point is for children to see that a whole group of objects can be composed of two or more parts and that they can represent this using a part-whole model. The group can be split in a variety of different ways. Draw children’s attention to the fact that the parts cannot be bigger than the whole group. Provide children with laminated part-whole models, so that they can experiment with physical objects – either drawing or placing pictures on the part-whole model. Encourage them to describe what they do by saying full sentences aloud. Children should be comfortable describing the parts and wholes in a variety of ways, sometimes starting with the whole and at other times with a part.

small_step_id: Year 1_5-6_Autumn__Place value within 10_2_Count objects
baseline_ss_wr_desc: The aim of this small step is for children to be able to fluently count to 10 when counting objects. Focus on the five counting principles when assessing children’s ability to count accurately. The one-to-one principle: Children assign one number name to each object that is being counted. The stable-order principle: When counting, the numbers have to be said in a certain order. The cardinal principle: The final object in a group is the total number of objects in that group. The abstraction principle: Anything can be counted, including things that cannot be touched, such as sounds and movements, for example jumps. The order-irrelevance principle: The order in which they count a group of objects is irrelevant. There will still be the same number.

baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this final small step, children explore missing number problems. They use the idea of inverse operations to see that if they start with a number and add 2 to it, then to “undo” that they need to subtract 2. Bar models and part-whole models are useful representations for this. “First, then, now” stories can be particularly helpful for children to act out the problems and visualise what is happening. Use of counters and ten frames, as well as number lines, supports children in their understanding of a missing number problem, helping them to discuss what the numbers in a problem represent. With the missing number problem 3 + = 5, a common mistake is to add 3 and 5 and get 3 + 8 = 5. Children need to spot that this does not make sense, as 8 is greater than 5

small_step_id: Year 1_5-6_Spring__Addition and subtraction within 20_1_Add by counting on within 20
baseline_ss_wr_desc: build on their learning from earlier in the year as they explore addition by counting on from a given number within 20 The use of ten frames and counters or cubes is particularly useful, together with bar models. Children should begin to understand that addition is commutative (although they do not need to formally know the word), and that it is more efficient to start from the greater number than the smaller number. For example, when working out 1 + 13, it is quicker to add 1 to 13 than to add 13 to 1. A number line is a particularly useful tool to exemplify this point, as children see the benefit of drawing just 1 jump rather than drawing 13 jumps. It is important that children see that they are not just counting the total of two separate numbers or items; rather, they are adding to what they already have.

small_step_id: Year 1_5-6_Spring__Addition and subtraction within 20_5_Near doubles
baseline_ss_wr_desc: Building on the previous step, in this small step children use doubles to help work out near doubles. For example, they can use the double fact that 6 + 6 = 12 to work out 6 + 7 by adding 1 more. They should see that this is a more efficient method than counting on. small_step_id: Year 1_5-6_Spring__Mass and volume_1_Heavier and lighter
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this block, children are formally introduced to mass for the first time. They may have some understanding of describing something as heavy or light from their own experience or from previous learning in Reception. Children begin by holding objects to compare them, using the language of “heavier” or “lighter”. They then use balance scales to check their comparisons. They need to understand that the heavier object is lower on the balance scale. At this stage, children do not need to measure the actual mass of objects in order to compare them. Children may assume that larger objects are heavier than smaller objects or that objects that are the same size/shape have the same mass. Comparing the mass of a large inflated balloon and a small ball of modelling clay, and comparing the mass of an inflated and a water-filled balloon should help to overcome these misconceptions.

baseline_ss_wr_desc: are asked to estimate for the first time. This is a new word for children to learn. Previously, they may have been asked to “guess” and make predictions. When children are beginning to estimate on a number line, take time to explore the halfway point. Where do they think halfway is? How do they know? What informal measurements could they use to check? For example, if they are estimating where 4 is on a blank number line from zero to 10, they need to be able to reason that it will be less than halfway.

They continue to explore and recognise the value of different denominations of coins. Discuss equivalence, showing children that a 20p coin is equivalent to twenty 1p coins and also two 10p coins. This helps them to see why we unitise and use coins with different values rather than using single pennies for everything. Once children are confident with recognising pence, introduce the £1 and £2 coins, explaining that they have a greater value than pence. Although children do not need to formally convert pounds to pence, it may be useful for them to see that £1 is equivalent to 100p. At this stage, children do not need to be introduced to the notation £ and p, as this is covered explicitly in Year 2

small_step_id: Year 1_5-6_Summer__Money_3_Recognise notes
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this step, children further develop their understanding of money by recognising and investigating the value of notes. Children use their understanding of place value to compare the value of different notes, for example recognising that a £20 note has a greater value than a £5 note because 20 > 5. They recognise that the larger the size of the note, the higher the value. Children explore how one note can have the value of many coins and/or notes. For example, a £10 note has the same value as two £5 notes or five £2 coins or ten £1 coins. Discuss why we use notes as well as coins. Children are less likely to have encountered a £50 note, as these are much less common in everyday life.

small_step_id: Year 1_5-6_Summer__Money_4_Count in coins
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In the previous small steps, children recognised and identified the value of coins and notes and saw how one note or coin could have the same value as a combination of a number of other notes or coins. Encourage children to draw coins or representations to match a given amount and use previous learning to compare amounts of money.

small_step_id: Year 1_5-6_Summer__Multiplication and division_1_Count in 2s
baseline_ss_wr_desc: explore counting both forwards and backwards in 2s. This builds on understanding from Autumn Block 2, when children added 1 and 2, as well as previous knowledge of doubles and finding 1 more and 1 less. Begin by practically exploring counting in 2s using things that come in pairs, such as socks and wheels on a bicycle. Number lines and a 1–50 number grid are useful representations that allow children to spot patterns when counting in 2s. They should count both forwards and backwards in 2s, but always starting from an even number. Begin to introduce children to the language of multiplication, for example “There are equal groups of 2. There are altogether.” This will be built on in future steps.

small_step_id: Year 1_5-6_Summer__Multiplication and division_4_Recognise equal groups
baseline_ss_wr_desc: begin by using stories that link to pictures and concrete resources to help support them in recognising equal groups. They recognise and explain how they know when there are equal groups and when there are not. In order to do this, children need to see lots of different examples of equal groups in different contexts, for example trays of buns or bunches of flowers. It is important for children to see equal groups that are arranged differently, so they understand that groups can look different but still be equal in number. For example, 5 dots arranged as on a dice, 5 dots in a row close together and 5 dots spaced further apart are all groups of 5 Children can begin to explore ways of making unequal groups equal by adding to or removing from some of the groups.

small_step_id: Year 1_5-6_Summer__Multiplication and division_5_Add equal groups
baseline_ss_wr_desc: use their knowledge from previous learning of recognising equal groups to now add equal groups together to find a total. Children focus on counting equal groups of 2, 5, and 10 and explore this within 50. They move on to identifying and recording the number sentence to match the groups. For example, show children 5 pairs of socks and allow them to represent them in a different way, such as with counters, then encourage them to write the number sentence to represent it: 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 10 At this point, children do not need to use the multiplication symbol and should record number sentences as repeated additions. However, they should be exposed to the language of multiplication, for example “There are 5 equal groups of 2, so there are 10 in total.”

small_step_id: Year 1_5-6_Summer__Multiplication and division_9_Make equal groups – sharing
baseline_ss_wr_desc: explore division in the form of sharing. Children first explore this practically using concrete resources and physically sharing them into groups. They should see that each group will then have the same amount. At this stage, children do not need to write number sentences using the division symbol, but they should be encouraged to explain what is happening using the language of division, for example “There are counters shared equally into groups. As an extension, children can look at situations where the objects cannot be shared equally and there are some left over.

small_step_id: Year 1_5-6_Summer__Place value within 100_6_Compare numbers with the same number of tens
small_step_name: Compare numbers with the same number of tens
baseline_ss_wr_desc: build on their learning from earlier in the year to compare numbers within 100. In previous blocks, children were introduced to the terms “greater than”, “less than” and “equal to” alongside the corresponding inequality symbols >, < and =. Children will need to practise using the words “fewer” and “less” accurately. Fewer is used when talking about a number of objects, whereas less is used when talking about values. Children use their understanding of the values of the digits in a 2-digit number to compare numbers with the same number of tens but a different number of ones. Encourage them to notice that when the tens digit is the same, they only need to compare the number of ones to decide which number is greater.

small_step_id: Year 1_5-6_Summer__Position and direction_1_Describe turns
baseline_ss_wr_desc: use the terms “full”, “half”, “quarter” and “three-quarter” to describe turns. They will be familiar with “half” and “quarter” from the previous block on fractions, but “three-quarter” will be a new concept to them. Children should be given lots of opportunities to practically turn objects as well as experience the motion of turns themselves. Children should investigate whether they can end up facing the same direction if they complete different turns, but they do not need to describe the direction of turns at this stage.

small_step_id: Year 1_5-6_Summer__Time_4_Hours, minutes and seconds
baseline_ss_wr_desc: develop their understanding of hours, minutes and seconds. Children learn that seconds are a shorter period of time than minutes and minutes are a shorter period of time than hours. Although they do not need to convert between different units, it is helpful for them to know that an hour is composed of 60 minutes and that a minute is composed of 60 seconds. Children make decisions about which unit of time would be most appropriate to measure a given activity. They compare time using vocabulary such as “quicker” and “slower”. When comparing durations, they need to understand that the smaller number of seconds, minutes or hours is the quicker time. Learning can be supported by practical investigations in which children use suitable equipment to measure the length of the activity, for example a stopwatch or a sand timer.

small_step_id: Year 1_5-6_Summer__Time_5_Tell the time to the hour
small_step_name: Tell the time to the hour
baseline_ss_wr_desc: are introduced to telling the time to the hour using an analogue clock. They are formally introduced to the term “o’clock” for the first time, although they may already have encountered this. Initially, children explore time using a number line and learn that an analogue clock face is a special type of number line. When pointing to numbers, ensure that the hand points exactly to the number and not to the side of it. Explain that when we use the word “hand”, we are referring to the arrow/pointer; this is specific to the topic of time. To begin with, children focus on reading time to the hour using only the hour hand. Once they are confident with this, they learn about the minute hand and that the hour hand is shorter than the minute hand. They recognise that when the minute hand is pointing directly to 12, they need to look at the shorter hand to see which hour it is.

small_step_id: Year 2_6-7_Autumn__Addition and subtraction_11_Subtract from a 10
baseline_ss_wr_desc: subtract a 1-digit number from any multiple of 10 within 100. Their knowledge of fact families for number bonds is particularly helpful here. For example, if they are calculating 50 − 6, they can use the fact that 6 + 4 = 10, so 10 − 6 = 4, and so 50 − 6 = 44 Rekenreks and number lines can be used to support children. Base 10 could be used, but might be less helpful for some children since they cannot physically break up the 10 rod. small_step_id: Year 2_6-7_Autumn__Addition and subtraction_20_Compare number sentences
baseline_ss_wr_desc: Children should already be familiar with the inequality symbols and in this small step they use them to compare number sentences. Encourage children to use correct mathematical language to say their answer in words, for example 4 + 7 > 4 + 5 should be said as “4 plus 7 is greater than 4 plus 5”. The focus of this small step is not just on working out the values of the calculations, but rather comparing the numbers within them. For example, when comparing 32 + 24 and 32 + 27, children do not need to work out both totals; instead, they should recognise that 32 is the same in each, and since 27 is greater than 24, this means that 32 + 27 is greater than 32 + 24 Children need to consider carefully when comparing subtractions, as even though 27 is greater than 24, 32 − 27 is not greater than 32 − 24, because they are subtracting more.

small_step_id: Year 2_6-7_Autumn__Addition and subtraction_3_Related facts
baseline_ss_wr_desc: use their knowledge of number bonds within 10, developed in the previous steps, to identify related facts for both addition and subtraction calculations. If children know that 2 + 5 = 7, then they should be able to use this knowledge to state that 20 + 50 = 70. Unitising tens and ones within a calculation can support children’s understanding and help to avoid common misconceptions. If 2 ones plus 5 ones is equal to 7 ones, then 2 tens plus 5 tens must be equal to 7 tens. This will avoid errors such as 20 + 50 = 700, which stems from thinking that there must be two zeros in the answer. Concrete resources can be used to support understanding of this. Base 10 is particularly useful and will support children in not only identifying the correct answer, but also using the correct vocabulary of tens and ones when explaining their answers.

baseline_ss_wr_desc: In the next few small steps, children explore in more detail the properties of 2-D shapes, starting by counting the number of sides. baseline_ss_wr_desc: Building from the previous small step, children count vertices on 2-D shapes. This is the first time that children have encountered the terms “vertex” and “vertices”. small_step_id: Year 2_6-7_Spring__Length and height_4_Order lengths and heights
baseline_ss_wr_desc: Building on the previous step, children now begin to order lengths and heights. The new language introduced in this step is “shortest”, “longest” and “tallest”, but they also continue to use “shorter”, “longer” and “taller” when describing the order of the objects. They order lengths from longest to shortest, heights from tallest to shortest and vice versa. Children order given lengths and heights, as well as objects that they have measured themselves. This supports children’s understanding of ordering numbers within 100, which they covered earlier in the year. Children could be stretched to ordering lengths and heights such as 30 cm, 15 cm and 30 m, where they need to consider the units for two values and the numerical values for the other two.

Children should first be shown representations, for example number pieces, of odd and even numbers that clearly show when a number can be divided into two whole equal parts and when it cannot. It may be useful to think of a definition for odd and even numbers and to identify non-examples as well as examples of both. Children should recognise that an even number can be halved to give a whole number answer, as it is divisible by 2 Once children are secure in their understanding of odd and even, they can recognise that they need to check the ones column of a number to decide whether it is odd or even.

small_step_id: Year 2_6-7_Summer__Fractions_15_Count in fractions up to a whole
small_step_name: Count in fractions up to a whole
baseline_ss_wr_desc: use their knowledge of unit fractions and non-unit fractions to count in fractions up to a whole, focusing on halves, thirds and quarters. This step is pictorially based and does not include number lines, which will be introduced in Year 3 Encourage children to recognise and represent fractions, as well as spotting patterns when counting. They should come to realise that the numerator increases, but the denominator stays the same. They should also be aware of examples in which a fraction is equivalent to 1 whole. Children do not need to count beyond 1 at this stage, but it may be useful to discuss that fractions do not stop at 1 whole.

small_step_id: Year 2_6-7_Summer__Fractions_1_Introduction to parts and whole
baseline_ss_wr_desc: This small step is the first time that children encounter fractions this year. They begin by learning about parts and wholes. Children are introduced to a variety of examples showing parts and wholes. It is important that they are secure in identifying the whole and parts of the whole. They can use everyday objects such as bicycles and flowers to identify the whole and parts of the whole. Using an interactive map is a good tool to identify the parts and whole, then zooming in to redefine the parts and whole before comparing. Children should also consider how many ways they can identify parts and wholes from pictures. They should begin to consider if the part is a large or small part of the whole. This learning will be built upon over the block, as children identify equal parts and begin to formally recognise and find fractions.

small_step_id: Year 2_6-7_Summer__Fractions_2_Equal and unequal parts
baseline_ss_wr_desc: explore equal and unequal parts. It is important that children have a secure understanding of the whole and parts before moving on to this step. They will already have used many skills required for this step in the multiplication and division block when identifying equal and unequal groups, so it may be useful to recap this. Children identify whether a shape has been split into equal or unequal parts. This is crucial learning, as it is used throughout the block to identify fractions. They first look at shapes where the equal parts look the same, but are then challenged to prove a shape has been split into equal parts where the parts do not look the same. At this stage, children do not need to describe the parts as fractions of the whole.

small_step_id: Year 2_6-7_Summer__Fractions_3_Recognise a half
baseline_ss_wr_desc: Children now begin to focus on specific fractions, starting with a half. Children were taught this in Year 1 and may be familiar with the word or concept of a half from everyday life. It could be useful to discuss this and identify any misconceptions, such as “the bigger half”. Once confident with their understanding of a half, they are introduced to the formal notation for fractions for the first time, in this case 1 2. It is important to spend time considering what each digit represents to support understanding, not only in this step, but for understanding of fractions moving forwards. Children are also introduced to the terms “numerator” and “denominator” for the first time. Children need to identify half of a shape, but they should also look at length and sets of objects. In the next step, they will work out half of a number.
