small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Autumn__Rates_1_Speed, distance and time
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students develop their understanding of the relationship between speed, distance and time, building on learning from Year 7 Remind students that speed is a compound measure. For example, express 60 mph as “60 miles travelled for every hour”, as this emphasises the meaning of “per” and why speed is described as a rate. Representations such as double number lines, bar models and ratio tables can be useful to highlight strategies to solve problems. Encourage students to focus on understanding the context of a question by looking at the units given. For example, a speed in km/h can be calculated by dividing the number of kilometres (distance) by the time.

small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Autumn__Rates_3_Flow problems and their graphs
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students explore flow problems by comparing how different-shaped containers are filled or drained. Start by comparing the filling of containers in the shape of prisms or cylinders with identical heights but differing bases, highlighting the effect that the shape has on how quickly it fills. Show that the graphs related to the time taken and depth of liquid in each container form a straight line, as the rate of flow is constant. Move on to containers with non-parallel sides, for example a conical or boiling flask, to draw out that the depth of the water will increase more quickly when the container is narrower and more slowly when it is wider. Show that, when plotted, changes in the width of the container are represented by a curve and form a non-linear graph.

small_step_name: Rates of change and their units

Explain that rates are compound measures, indicating that one unit changes relative to another, for example metres per second, litres per minute. Encourage students to think of rates as “ per ”, where time is often a factor, but not always (for example, cost of fuel per mile travelled). Emphasise the importance of interpreting the gradient of a graph in context, linking the concept of rate of change to the gradient.

small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Autumn__Standard form_1_Numbers in standard form
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students build on their knowledge of standard form from Year 8, revisiting conversion to and from standard form, as well as solving problems with standard form. Remind students of the correct form: A × 10n, where 1 ≤ A < 10 and n is an integer. Students need to be able to recognise when a number is in standard form. This can be encouraged through presenting numbers such as 12.6 × 105 and asking them to convert to standard form. A place value chart can be used to support students’ understanding of standard form, if appropriate. Using numbers in context, such as populations and bacteria, helps to highlight why standard form is an efficient way to write large or small numbers.

small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Autumn__Standard form_2_Compare and order numbers in standard form
small_step_name: Compare and order numbers in standard form
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students compare and order numbers given in standard form, ordinary form and words. Discuss strategies for comparing numbers, such as starting by considering the powers of 10. Students should recognise that they do not always need to convert to ordinary form. Instead, they can compare the powers of 10 or, if the two numbers have the same power of 10, they can compare the value of A. Revisiting ordering decimal numbers will help to avoid any misconceptions that may be a barrier to ordering numbers in standard form. Place value charts can be used to deepen students’ understanding.

small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Spring__Algebraic manipulation_1_Expand single brackets and simplify
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students review how to expand and simplify expressions involving single brackets. Students should have prior knowledge of expanding and simplifying expressions of the form 3 ± 4x(x ± 5) and 3(x ± 2) ± 4x(x ± 5). Remind them that each term inside the bracket must be multiplied by the coefficient of the bracket before simplifying. Ensure that they are confident working with both positive and negative terms. Area models and algebra tiles can be a helpful visual tool for representing expressions and supporting understanding. As confidence develops, students can progress to expressions with more algebraic terms, for example a(2a + 3b) − a(4a − 5b).

small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Spring__Algebraic manipulation_3_Expand double brackets
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students expand double brackets of the form (x ± a)(x ± b), sometimes referred to as expanding a pair of binomials. Students may have encountered this learning in Year 8 as an extend step. Using the grid method alongside algebra tiles can help students to make connections when multiplying terms, particularly by reinforcing links with the area model. Start with expressions using only positive terms to build understanding. Once students are confident, move on to brackets involving negative terms. Encourage students to explore unfamiliar forms, such as (x + 5)2 or (x + 3)(4 + x). Introducing and discussing the term “quadratic” will support them with making links to quadratic graphs.

small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Spring__Algebraic manipulation_4_Expand more complex double brackets
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students build on their learning from the previous step to explore double brackets of the form (ax ± b)(cx ± d). Students need a secure understanding of algebraic simplification and operations involving negative numbers. Start with only positive terms within the expression, before introducing negative terms. Recap the use of an area model as a visual prompt to support discussion on expanding double brackets, using algebra tiles if necessary. Expressions in unfamiliar forms such as (3x + 2)2 or (3x + 2)(3 + 5x) could also be explored. As in the previous step, discuss the word “quadratic” to help students make links to quadratic graphs.

small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Spring__Algebraic manipulation_5_Use identities
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students build on their understanding of simplifying expressions and expanding single and double brackets by applying this knowledge to algebraic identities. Students learn to identify and use identities to determine unknown values. At this stage, they should begin to recognise that in an identity, the coefficients of matching terms on both sides must be equal, for example if ax + by æ 5x + y, then a = 5 and b = 1. Using a Frayer model can help students explore the key features of an identity and differentiate it from equations and expressions, with non-examples being particularly useful for clarity. Start with simple identities such as 1 2a æ a ÷ 2, then move on to more complex examples that involve simplifying and comparing coefficients to solve for unknowns.

If appropriate, challenge students to factorise quadratics in unfamiliar forms, for example 20 + x − x2

baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this extend step, students solve quadratic equations of the form x2 + bx + c by first factorising, building on their prior understanding of both factorising quadratic expressions and solving linear equations. Recap how to factorise quadratic expressions with positive and negative terms, ensuring that students are confident with the process. Demonstrate this using simple examples such as ab = 0. Reinforce that factorised quadratic expressions typically lead to two solutions and highlight the connection between the factors and the roots of the equation.

small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Spring__Constructions and congruence_1_Draw and measure angles
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students revisit using a protractor to draw and measure angles accurately and use angle notation, which is essential for subsequent steps in this block. Remind students how to line up a protractor correctly when drawing or measuring, ensuring that they use the correct scale. Encourage them to estimate the sizes of angles before measuring and to think about whether they are acute, obtuse or reflex angles. Students also explore strategies to draw or measure reflex angles, such as creating a 300° angle by drawing a 60° angle and indicating that the greater of the two angles created is 300°.

baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students use a pair of compasses to accurately construct triangles where three side lengths are given (SSS). Model constructing a triangle with three known side lengths. Emphasise correct placement of the compass point and smooth, steady arcs, as well as measuring the compass width accurately using a ruler. Encourage them to use a ruler to check the accuracy of their constructed triangle.

small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Spring__Constructions and congruence_4_Construct an angle bisector
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students bisect an angle using a pair of compasses. Establish that bisecting an angle means that an angle is split into two equal angles. For example, bisecting a 60° angle results in two 30° angles. Once students are confident in bisecting a single angle, present them with other problems, for example bisecting an angle in a polygon. They should also be given opportunities to bisect angles in a given context, for example using an angle bisector to identify a region closer to one side than another in a polygon. Ensure that students keep all construction lines when constructing angle bisectors.

baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students build on learning from earlier in the block to explore various ways in which adults can borrow money, including bank loans, payday loans and credit cards. This step will help students to consider the potential consequences of borrowing, including the impact of missed repayments.

small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Spring__Maths and money_11_Spending overseas
baseline_ss_wr_desc: This small step focuses on the financial implications of spending overseas, with students exploring exchange rates, currency conversions and different payment options. Key considerations when travelling overseas are sales tax, the difference between paying with cash or card and phone charges. Compare paying in local currency with students’ own currency and how it affects the total cost, depending on bank and vendor exchange rates. Discuss how if no charge is set by the bank for paying in a different currency, then paying in local currency can be more cost effective, but it depends on the exchange rates that are set by both the bank and vendor. It can be helpful to highlight that British pounds (£), Great British pounds (GBP) and sterling all refer to the same currency. Students may see these terms used in different contexts, especially when comparing exchange rates or making payments abroad.

small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Spring__Maths and money_12_Insurance
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students continue to apply maths in a range of contexts as they explore insurance. Discuss different types of insurance in everyday life, for example car, travel, household and life insurance. Students examine the financial implications of insurance, including learning about insurance premium tax (IPT). IPT is applied to most general insurance policies, except life insurance. Students look at the standard 12% rate for home, car and pet insurance and the higher 20% rate for travel and mechanical repair insurance, such as boiler cover. They explore the idea of excess and consider how a lower premium does not always mean a better deal. It is also important to discuss how some types of insurance, such as car insurance, are mandatory, while others are optional and may depend on individual circumstances or financial situations.

small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Spring__Ratio and proportion_6_Solve problems with ratio and algebra E
small_step_name: Solve problems with ratio and algebra E
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students make links between equivalent ratios where one of the ratios contains algebraic expressions. Begin with algebraic ratios equivalent to 1 : 1, for example x + 3 : 7 = 1 : 1. Highlight that this means that the parts are equal, so x + 3 and 7 are equal and an equation can be formed and solved (x + 3 = 7). Move on to algebraic ratios equivalent to other unitary ratios, for example 2x : 24 = 1 : 2, emphasising that 2x 24. Discuss the relationships between the parts in the ratio, for example “The second part of the ratio is double the first part.” As in previous steps, bar models may be a useful support for students to form equations. If appropriate, students could explore algebraic ratios equivalent to non-unitary ratios, for example 2x : x + 8 = 2 : 3

small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Spring__Straight line graphs_1_Lines parallel to the axes, y = x and y = −x
small_step_name: Lines parallel to the axes, y = x and y = −x
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students revisit and extend learning of equations of lines parallel to the axes and the lines y = x and y = −x. Start with lines parallel to the axes before moving on to y = x and y = −x, ensuring that students can both plot and recognise the lines. It is important that they understand that the equation of a line describes a relationship between any pair of coordinates on that line. For example, any point on the line y = 3 will have a y-coordinate of 3. Similarly, any point on the line y = −x will have coordinates of the form (−a, a) or (a, −a). Draw attention to the x-axis being the line y = 0 and the y-axis being the line x = 0

small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Spring__Straight line graphs_2_Explore gradients
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students explore gradients of straight line graphs and learn that the value of m in the equation y = mx + c represents the gradient of the line. Start with lines of the form y = mx for both positive and negative values of m, before exploring lines of the form y = mx + c. Recap plotting graphs from a table of values before moving on to sketches of lines and comparing gradients. Draw attention to how the value of m affects the steepness of the line. Students should find gradients of lines on coordinate grids in preparation for finding the equation of a line from a graph. In this step, it is not necessary to investigate values of c, as this is explored in the next step. Graph-plotting software can be a useful tool to support student understanding.

small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Spring__Straight line graphs_3_Explore intercepts
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students explore how the value of c affects a line. Start with lines of the form y = x + c, highlighting that the value of c is the point at which a line intercepts the y-axis, before exploring lines of the form y = mx + c. Establish that the value of c gives the coordinates of the y-intercept, (0, c). Show that in y = mx + c, y = c when x = 0, reminding students that the equation of the y-axis is x = 0. Highlight the special case of lines of the form y = mx and the related y-intercept, (0, 0). Discuss the equivalence of equations such as y = 3x − 2 and y = 3x + −2. Graph-plotting software can be a useful tool to support students’ understanding.

small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Spring__Straight line graphs_4_y = mx + c
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students combine learning from previous steps to interpret equations of lines given in the form y = mx + c, identifying both the gradient, m, and the y-intercept, (0, c). Build students’ confidence in identifying the values of m and c from equations in the form y = mx + c, before introducing non-standard examples such as y = 6 − 2x and 3x + 2 = y. It is not necessary to look at more complex rearrangements of the equation, such as 2y = 3x + 4, as this will be explored in a later step. Students also build on their understanding that lines with the same gradient are parallel and use this knowledge to write equations of parallel lines.

small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Spring__Straight line graphs_5_Rearrange equations to the form y = mx + c E
small_step_name: Rearrange equations to the form y = mx + c E
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this extend step, students apply their knowledge of rearranging formulae to writing equations in the form y = mx + c. Start with formulae that require one step of rearrangement, for example 2y = 6x + 8, before moving on to more complex rearrangements such as 8x + 2y =10. Ensure that students explore examples where they rearrange equations and then write the gradients and y-intercepts. Emphasise the necessity of writing equations in the form y = mx + c in order to identify the gradient and y-intercept. Students could also explore parallel lines in rearranged formulae. At this stage, it is not necessary to look at examples of equations where y is negative, for example 4x = 7 − y.

small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Spring__Straight line graphs_6_Find the equation of a line from a graph
small_step_name: Find the equation of a line from a graph
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students combine their knowledge of finding gradients and y-intercepts to write equations of straight lines from a given graph. Remind students how to calculate the gradient from a graph. Drawing a right-angled triangle between two points on the line and then dividing the vertical distance by the horizontal distance is a useful strategy. Encourage students to examine the scales on axes carefully before calculating gradients. Ensure that they have opportunities to work with fractional and negative gradients and negative y-intercepts.

small_step_name: Interpret gradients and intercepts of real-life graphs
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students apply their knowledge of finding gradients and y-intercepts of lines to finding and interpreting the gradients and y-intercepts of graphs in context. Exemplify the difference between finding the gradient and y-intercept and interpreting them in context. For example, in a graph representing the cost of a taxi journey for a given number of miles, the gradient represents the cost per mile and the y-intercept represents the minimum fare. Students should see examples where the graph demonstrates direct proportion and examples where it does not, understanding that direct proportion graphs start at the point (0, 0). Discuss why the graphs only show positive values of x and y.

baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this extend step, students apply their knowledge of lines parallel to the axes and the lines y = x and y = − x to draw and shade inequalities such as x > 3 and y ≤ x. Inequalities on number lines can help to illustrate the connection between open circles, used to represent “less than” or “greater than”, and dashed lines, which indicate that boundary values are not included. Start with regions for single inequalities such as y ≥ 5 before introducing double inequalities, for example −2 < x ≤ 3. Explore the regions of inequalities such as y > x and y > −x, but not more complex inequalities such as y > 2x + 3. Encourage students to test a point to check their solution.

baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students interpret quadratic graphs by reading values from them. Establish that it is only possible to find one value of y for a given value of x, but potentially two values of x for a given value of y. Highlight that values are identified by finding the intersection of two graphs. For example, drawing the graphs of y = x2 + 5x + 6 and y = 2 will identify the values of x when y = 2 This step focuses on reading values from a quadratic graph. Students will interpret roots, intercepts and turning points in a later extend step, although some of this content can be combined here, if appropriate. Dynamic graphing software can be useful to support understanding. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may give only one value of x for a given value of y, when there should be two values of x. • Students may read from the wrong axis for solutions. • Students may struggle to read estimates for non-integer coordinates. • Inaccurately drawn graphs may cause inaccurate results when reading values. small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Summer__Non-linear graphs_7_Interpret cubic graphs (E)
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this extend step, students build on their understanding from the previous step to interpret cubic graphs. Emphasise that for a given value of x, there is always a unique corresponding value of y, but for a given value of y, there may be one, two or three corresponding values of x. Highlight that, unlike quadratic graphs, cubic graphs always have at least one value of x for any value of y. Using graphs to solve equations is not essential at this stage, but relevant links can be made, such as finding the values of x when y = 0, if appropriate. Dynamic graphing software remains a valuable tool to visualise these features and to support students in recognising the general shape and behaviour of different cubic functions. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may give only one value of x for a given value of y, when they should give two or three values. • Students may read from the wrong axis for solutions. • Students may struggle to read estimates for non-integer coordinates. • Inaccurately drawn graphs may cause inaccurate results when reading values. baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students build on their understanding of square numbers and square roots, together with their knowledge of solving equations, to solve equations with square numbers and square roots. Recap calculating square numbers and their square roots. Students apply this knowledge to solve equations that involve squares and square roots, for example x2 = 16 or x = 5. Emphasise the use of inverse operations to solve the equations and highlight why x2 = 16 has two solutions: x = 4 and x = −4. Explain that both 42 = 16 and (−4)2 = 16, so the equation has two values of x that make it true. Therefore, when solving x2 = a, they are looking for all values whose square is a, which includes both the positive and negative values. As students increase in confidence, they move on to solving equations with coefficients that are not 1 and with numbers on both sides of the equation. small_step_name: Use Pythagoras’ theorem on coordinate axes
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students build on their knowledge of coordinates by using Pythagoras’ theorem to find the length of a line segment between two points. Start in the first quadrant, drawing a line segment and counting the horizontal and vertical distances to form a right-angled triangle. Use these to apply Pythagoras’ theorem. As confidence grows, sketch coordinates without a grid and ask students how they could calculate the length without counting squares. Encourage clear diagram labelling, accurate subtraction of coordinates and interpreting results in context. Students can then progress to working with all four quadrants and reason about distances without always using a diagram. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may square the coordinates instead of the distances between them. • Students may mix up the order of subtraction or make arithmetic errors with directed numbers when finding horizontal and vertical differences. • Students may use the formula for finding the midpoint of a line or the gradient instead of using Pythagoras’ theorem. • Students may misidentify the sides that form the right-angled triangle on the grid. National Curriculum links • Use Pythagoras’ theorem and trigonometric ratios in similar triangles to solve problems involving right-angled triangles Mathematical talk • What shape is formed if you draw a horizontal and vertical line from each point? • How can you use the right-angled triangle to find the length of the line segment? • Which side lengths of the triangle do you know, and which are you trying to find? • How can the side lengths of the right-angled triangle be calculated from the coordinates? baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this extend step, students explore a range of proofs for Pythagoras’ theorem. Algebraic and geometric proofs are examples of proofs that can be explored. It is useful to begin by using a visual or dynamic demonstration to make the result feel intuitive, before introducing a more formal algebraic or geometric proof. Perigal’s dissection was introduced in Step 3, when students were using the theorem to determine whether a triangle is right-angled, and it may be beneficial to refer back to this to support understanding. This step is an opportunity to revisit the proof in a richer context and highlight that Pythagoras’ theorem is not just a formula to memorise, but a result with multiple clear and convincing justifications. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may believe that a proof must always involve numbers, not general cases with algebra or geometry. • Students may think that all proofs look the same, not recognising that multiple types, such as algebraic, geometric and visual proofs, exist. National Curriculum links • Use Pythagoras’ theorem and trigonometric ratios in similar triangles to solve problems involving right-angled triangles • Apply angle facts, triangle congruence, similarity and properties of quadrilaterals to derive results about angles and sides, including Pythagoras’ theorem, and use known results to obtain simple proofs Mathematical talk • What do you notice about how the shapes are arranged in this proof? • What is the same and what is different before and after the rearrangement? • Why does rearranging the shapes not change the total area? • Which parts of the diagram represent a2, b2 and c2? • How does the diagram help you to understand why a2 + b2 = c2? • What assumptions are being made in this proof? • How do you know that this works for all right-angled triangles, not just this one? • Do you think that one proof is more convincing or clearer than the others? small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Summer__Pythagoras theorem_8_Pythagoras’ theorem in 3-D shapes E
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this step, students extend their understanding of Pythagoras’ theorem into three dimensions. Start with cubes or cuboids and use physical or digital 3-D models to support visualisation of the right-angled triangles within them. Guide students through the two-stage process, first using Pythagoras’ theorem to find the length of a diagonal, then applying it again to find the length of the next diagonal. Once they are confident, students could derive the general formula d = l2 + w2 + ℎ2 , where d is the diagonal and l, w and h are the edge lengths of the cuboid. Prompt them to compare the step-by-step method with the formula, recognising how it simplifies repeated application. If appropriate, students can apply their understanding to other 3-D shapes, identifying right-angled triangles within pyramids and cylinders. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may have difficulty visualising right angles and/or diagonal lengths in 3-D shapes. • Students may incorrectly use two edges that do not meet at a right angle. Which one is the hypotenuse? • Why might drawing a right-angled triangle be useful when finding the length of a diagonal in a 3-D shape? • What is the greatest distance between the vertices of a cube? • How many times do you need to use Pythagoras’ theorem to work out the length of this diagonal? • Why is applying Pythagoras’ theorem twice in a cuboid the same as the formula d = l2 + w2 + ℎ2 ? • What is the longest diagonal length of the room that you are in? baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students explore probabilities using Venn diagrams. Recap the regions of a Venn diagram, clarifying how each represents a distinct group within the data. Draw students’ attention to how probabilities are calculated, by comparing the number of outcomes in a region with the total represented by the diagram. If appropriate, students could explore the “given that” clause, finding the probability of one event when another is already known to have occurred. This introduces conditional probability in a structured way and highlights how Venn diagrams make relationships between events visual. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may omit elements written outside the circles. • Students may forget to include the intersection when calculating the probability of “A or B”. • Students may think that the total in the denominator should be the sum of the two circles, rather than the overall total. • When answering “given that” questions, students may use the total population instead of restricting it to the given condition. baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students identify and represent sets and begin to use set notation. Use familiar examples, such as the set of even numbers, to model what a set looks like. Explain that each number or object is called an element or member of the set. Encourage the use of correct notation, such as writing a set using curly brackets, for example { 2, 3, 5, 7 }. As students’ confidence develops, introduce the concept of the universal set, denoted by the Greek letter ξ (pronounced “ksi”), as the complete collection of numbers/objects under consideration. Model how other sets can be seen as subsets of the universal set. For example, if ξ is the set of integers 1 to 10 inclusive, then { 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 } is a subset of ξ. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may not be specific enough or may omit details when describing a set. • Students may confuse the universal set with all numbers/ objects rather than understanding it as the complete collection of numbers/objects under consideration. • Students may think that sets can only be numerical. small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Summer__Sets and probability_3_Union of a set
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students are introduced to the union of two or more sets and its representation using set notation. Explain that the union of two sets means combining all of the elements from both, with no repetitions. Use the symbol to represent the union and clearly model examples, for example if A = { 1, 2, 3 } and B = { 3, 4, 5 }, A B = { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 }. Demonstrate how the union can be represented visually using Venn diagrams by shading both circles to represent all the elements included. Reinforce that the union always brings together every element from the sets under consideration. Draw students’ attention to the difference between union and intersection by considering how they differ in symbolic, written and visual representations. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may mix up the symbols and or use them interchangeably. • Students may list repeated elements when combining sets, for example A B = { 1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5 }. • Students may not include the members of an intersection when listing the members of a union. National Curriculum links • Enumerate sets and unions/intersections of sets systematically, using tables, grids and Venn diagrams Mathematical talk • What does A B mean? How can you show A B on a Venn diagram? • How do you read A B out loud? • What part of the diagram should be shaded? • How does the shading show “in A or in B or in both”? • Does the union include the elements that are in both sets? Explain how you know. • If A = { a, b, c } and B = { c, d, e }, what are the elements of A B? Explain your answer. • If ξ = { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 }, A = { 1, 2, 3 } and B = { 2, 3, 4 }, what are the elements of A B? Explain your answer. • How is the union different from the intersection? • Can a union of two sets ever have fewer elements than either set on its own? Explain your answer. • Is the union of two sets always bigger than their intersection? Explain your answer. Union of sets Year 9 | Summer term | Block 3 – Sets and probability | Step 3

small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Summer__Sets and probability_4_Complement of a set (E)
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this extend step, students explore the complement of a set and its representation using set notation. Remind students that the universal set, ξ, is the complete collection of objects or numbers under consideration. Explain that the complement of a set contains all the elements in the universal set that are not in a set. Use clear examples to model this idea; for example, if ξ is the set of integers from 1 to 10 inclusive and A = { 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 }, then the complement of A, written as A′, is { 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 }. Encourage students to write complements using set notation and to describe them in words, such as “the set of integers from 1 to 10 that are not even”. As students gain confidence, highlight how complements help them to see how sets and their opposites fit within the universal set. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may try to take the complement of a set without reference to the universal set, ξ, leading to inconsistent answers. • Students may think that complement means the “opposite”, rather than exclusion. National Curriculum links • Enumerate sets and unions/intersections of sets systematically, using tables, grids and Venn diagrams Mathematical talk • What does A′ mean? How can you show A′ on a Venn diagram? • How do you read A′ out loud? • What is meant by the “universal set, ξ ”? • Do all sets have a complement? • What is the relationship between the complement of a set, the set itself and the universal set? • Can a set of non-numerical elements have a complement? Explain your answer. • If A = { 2, 4, 6 } and ξ = { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 }, what is A′ ? • Does A′ ever include elements from A? Explain your answer. • What is the same and what is different about a complement and an intersection/union? • If ξ is the set of students in a class and A is the set of students with a packed lunch, what does A′ represent? small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Summer__Sets and probability_5_Probability of a single event ​
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students consolidate and build on learning from Year 8, using probability notation such as P(heads), expressing probabilities as fractions, decimals and percentages, and using the property that probabilities sum to 1 Introduce mutually exclusive events through simple cases, such as rolling a 2 or a 6 on a dice, to illustrate how probabilities can be added. When they are confident, students apply these skills to problem solving in ratio and algebraic contexts. For example, they may work with ratio and convert it into a fraction, or use algebra to represent unknown probabilities and solve equations. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may describe the probability in words rather than calculating it as a fraction/decimal/percentage. • Students may use incorrect total outcomes when interpreting word problems. • Students may think that all probabilities are mutually exclusive. • Students may express a probability as a ratio. National Curriculum links • Record, describe and analyse the frequency of outcomes of simple probability experiments involving randomness, fairness, equally and unequally likely outcomes, using appropriate language and the 0–1 probability scale • Understand that the probabilities of all possible outcomes sum to 1 Mathematical talk • What does “P(heads)” mean? • What does “random” mean? • Why must the outcomes be equally likely for this method to work? • Explain how to calculate the probability of a single event. • What does it mean when two events are mutually exclusive? • Is drawing a red card and drawing a king from a pack of cards an example of mutually exclusive events? Explain your answer. • Give an example of two events that are/are not mutually exclusive. • If the ratio of blue to red counters is 7 : 3, what is the probability of selecting a red counter when a counter is selected at random? small_step_name: Use diagrams to work out probabilities
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students use two-way tables, frequency trees and sample space diagrams to work out probabilities. Explore one diagram at a time. Model how outcomes in a two-way table are placed in rows and columns so that totals can be completed and used to find probabilities. Use sample space diagrams to display every outcome and identify subsets representing events. Recap frequency trees to show how information is organised step by step, with branches leading to totals. Emphasise how each diagram organises information clearly to support accurate calculations. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may not identify the correct event, total or subset from a diagram, leading to errors when calculating probabilities. • Students may include the wrong numerical values from the diagram. • In sample space diagrams, students may treat a single outcome as equivalent to an event, leading to an incorrect probability. National Curriculum links • Generate theoretical sample spaces for single and combined events with equally likely, mutually exclusive outcomes and use these to calculate theoretical probabilities Mathematical talk • How do you interpret a two-way table? What values do you know that can help you work out unknown information? • What does this total represent, and how is it different from an individual cell? • Why is a sample space diagram helpful for listing all the possible outcomes? • How is this two-way table similar to a frequency tree? • What does each branch represent on a frequency tree? • How do the totals at the end of each branch help you to calculate probabilities? • How many outcomes are there in total? • Can the same probability be found using more than one diagram? • To work out the probability of , which numbers in the table do you need to use? small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Summer__Sets and probability_7_Relative frequency
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students explore relative frequency through experiments and recorded results. Emphasise how the relative frequency of an outcome fluctuates with a small number of trials, but as more trials are completed it stabilises. This shows the link between probability and relative frequency, with probability seen as the value that relative frequency approaches in the long run. Discuss how short-term variation becomes less significant as the number of trials increases, so results move closer to the theoretical probability, making larger samples more reliable. Graphs can make these patterns clearer, and computer simulations allow students to see behaviour. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may think that relative frequency and probability are the same. • Students may not recognise that conducting more trials increases the accuracy of the relative frequency. • Students may think that results should reflect theoretical probability after only a few trials, without recognising the effect of short-term variation. • Students may think that if an outcome has not occurred for a while, then it is certain to happen soon. National Curriculum links • Record, describe and analyse the frequency of outcomes of simple probability experiments involving randomness, fairness, equally and unequally likely outcomes, using appropriate language and the 0–1 probability scale Mathematical talk • How is relative frequency calculated? How is it different from probability? • Why is relative frequency called “experimental probability”? • Can relative frequency ever be greater than 1? Explain how you know. • Why is relative frequency not exactly the same each time? • Why is experimental probability different from theoretical probability? • If you roll a dice six times, will you definitely roll a 4? What might happen if the dice is rolled sixty times? How would the proportion of 4s compare to when the dice was only rolled six times? • A dice is rolled twenty times and lands on 4 five times. What is the relative frequency of rolling a 4? • What happens to experimental and theoretical probability when a very large number of trials has been completed? Relative frequency Year 9 | Summer term | Block 3 – Sets and probability | Step 7

small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Summer__Sets and probability_8_Expected outcomes
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students explore expected outcomes, building on their knowledge of relative frequency and experimental probability. Highlight that expected outcomes represent a long-term average, rather than a precise prediction for individual trials. Variability can be illustrated through experiments, showing that results may differ from the calculated expectation, particularly with smaller samples. For example, if the probability of rolling a 6 on a fair dice is 1 6, then in 60 rolls the expected outcome would be ten 6s, although the actual result may vary. Ensure that students practise calculating expected outcomes when probabilities are expressed as fractions, decimals or percentages, and compare these with experimental results. Using tables, graphs or simulations helps to make the patterns more visible and reinforces the link between expected outcomes and probability. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may think that the expected outcome is what will happen in practice, rather than an estimation. • Students may believe that variation from the expected outcome means that the calculation is incorrect. National Curriculum links • Record, describe and analyse the frequency of outcomes of simple probability experiments involving randomness, fairness, equally and unequally likely outcomes, using appropriate language and the 0–1 probability scale. Mathematical talk • What does “expected outcome” mean? • If the probability of an event is 1 4, how many times would you expect it to occur in 40 trials? How many times would you expect it to occur in 400/4000 trials? • Can the actual results be different from the expected results? Explain your answer. • Why might results from a small number of trials look different from the expected outcome? • How does increasing the number of trials affect how close results are to the expected outcome? • What might it suggest if the expected outcome is 25 but the result is 40? • How could you use expected outcomes to check whether a game is fair? Year 9_13-14_Summer__Sets and probability_9_Independent events
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students explore independent events. It can be helpful to introduce the idea through a sample space diagram, for example for rolling two dice, where all possible outcomes can be listed and favourable cases counted. Draw students’ attention to how this method produces the same result as multiplying the separate probabilities, for example 1 2 × 1 6 = 1 12 for rolling an even number on one dice and a 5 on the other. Making this connection explains why multiplication is used for independent events and helps to link different approaches. Encourage students to express probabilities as both fractions and decimals, supporting fluency and making comparisons easier. Using diagrams provides opportunities for students to develop accurate reasoning. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may think that “independent” means that the probabilities are equal, rather than that one outcome does not affect the other. • Students may confuse independent with mutually exclusive events, not recognising that mutually exclusive outcomes cannot happen together. National Curriculum links • Generate theoretical sample spaces for single and combined events with equally likely, mutually exclusive outcomes and use these to calculate theoretical probabilities Mathematical talk • What does “independent event” mean? • Give an example of two events that are independent. • Can two events be independent if one is much more likely than the other? • If I roll one dice and you roll another, does my result affect yours? Explain your answer. • How is independence different from fairness? • Can an event be unfair but still independent? Give an example. • Can two independent events happen at the same time? Explain your answer. • Can two mutually exclusive events happen at the same time? Explain your answer. • How does this difference change how you calculate their probabilities? • If the probability of winning a game is 0.3, what is the probability of winning twice in a row? topic: Solve equations with squares and square roots
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students build on their understanding of square numbers and square roots, together with their knowledge of solving equations, to solve equations with square numbers and square roots. Recap calculating square numbers and their square roots. Students apply this knowledge to solve equations that involve squares and square roots, for example x2 = 16 or x = 5. Emphasise the use of inverse operations to solve the equations and highlight why x2 = 16 has two solutions: x = 4 and x = −4. Explain that both 42 = 16 and (−4)2 = 16, so the equation has two values of x that make it true. Therefore, when solving x2 = a, they are looking for all values whose square is a, which includes both the positive and negative values. As students increase in confidence, they move on to solving equations with coefficients that are not 1 and with numbers on both sides of the equation.

baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students identify the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle. Start with several right-angled triangles and ask students to measure the length of each side. Encourage them to identify the side that is opposite the right angle and ask what they notice about its length compared to the other sides. Introduce the term “hypotenuse” and emphasise that this is always the longest side in a right-angled triangle and is always opposite the right angle. Include plenty of examples in different orientations, so that they do not rely on position or direction. Include non-examples to challenge misconceptions. As students develop confidence, ask them to identify the hypotenuses within a compound shape made up of right-angled triangles.

small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Summer__Solve equations with squares and square roots_3_Pythagoras’ theorem (find the hypotenuse)
topic: Solve equations with squares and square roots
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students explore Pythagoras’ theorem and use it to identify right-angled triangles. Start by exploring the areas of the squares on each side of a right-angled triangle. Use concrete or visual representations to support students in discovering that the sum of the areas on the two shorter sides is equal to the area on the side of the hypotenuse. Guide students to notice and articulate this relationship, leading to the formulation of Pythagoras’ theorem, a2 + b2 = c2. Emphasise that the hypotenuse is represented by “c” or “hyp”. Once students understand the connection, ask them to apply the rule to check whether a given triangle is right-angled, using known side lengths to test if the condition is satisfied.

small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Summer__Solve equations with squares and square roots_4_Pythagoras’ theorem (find any side)
topic: Solve equations with squares and square roots
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students calculate the length of the hypotenuse, given the two shorter sides, building on their knowledge that the hypotenuse is the side opposite the right angle and that it is the longest side in a right-angled triangle. Start with right-angled triangles in a variety of orientations, encouraging students to identify the hypotenuse before substituting values into the formula a2 + b2 = c2. Emphasise the importance of squaring correctly, adding accurately and remembering to take the square root as the final step. Remind students that answers should often be rounded to a given degree of accuracy, for example 1 decimal place. Encourage students to check whether their answer makes sense by comparing it to the lengths of the other sides. As their confidence develops, introduce problems involving compound shapes, where identifying right-angled triangles is required.

small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Summer__Solve equations with squares and square roots_5_Use Pythagoras’ theorem on coordinate axes
topic: Solve equations with squares and square roots
small_step_name: Use Pythagoras’ theorem on coordinate axes
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students deepen their understanding of Pythagoras’ theorem by applying it to find the length of any side in a right-angled triangle. Remind students how to identify the hypotenuse and to understand that, when the hypotenuse and one shorter side are known, they need to subtract the square of the shorter side from the square of the hypotenuse before taking the square root. Use diagrams and model the reasoning aloud to support students’ understanding so that they do not simply rely on memorised steps. Once they are confident, introduce questions where the unknown side is sometimes the hypotenuse and sometimes a shorter side. This encourages students to think carefully about which side they are finding and helps to secure a deeper conceptual understanding of the theorem.

small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Summer__Solve equations with squares and square roots_6_Proofs of Pythagoras’ theorem E
topic: Solve equations with squares and square roots
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students build on their knowledge of coordinates by using Pythagoras’ theorem to find the length of a line segment between two points. Start in the first quadrant, drawing a line segment and counting the horizontal and vertical distances to form a right-angled triangle. Use these to apply Pythagoras’ theorem. As confidence grows, sketch coordinates without a grid and ask students how they could calculate the length without counting squares. Encourage clear diagram labelling, accurate subtraction of coordinates and interpreting results in context. Students can then progress to working with all four quadrants and reason about distances without always using a diagram.

small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Summer__Solve equations with squares and square roots_7_Pythagoras’ theorem in 3-D shapes E
topic: Solve equations with squares and square roots
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this extend step, students explore a range of proofs for Pythagoras’ theorem. Algebraic and geometric proofs are examples of proofs that can be explored. It is useful to begin by using a visual or dynamic demonstration to make the result feel intuitive, before introducing a more formal algebraic or geometric proof. Perigal’s dissection was introduced in Step 3, when students were using the theorem to determine whether a triangle is right-angled, and it may be beneficial to refer back to this to support understanding. This step is an opportunity to revisit the proof in a richer context and highlight that Pythagoras’ theorem is not just a formula to memorise, but a result with multiple clear and convincing justifications.

small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Summer__Transformations_10_""0 Reflection
Year 9_13-14_Summer__Transformations_10_Reflection
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students build on their understanding from Year 8, completing and describing reflections in horizontal, vertical and diagonal lines. Some students may not yet have encountered reflections in lines expressed algebraically, or fully described reflections, as these are covered in extend steps in Year 8 Recap how to identify equations of vertical, horizontal and diagonal lines, as this underpins both drawing and describing reflections. Emphasise that a full description must include both the fact that it is a reflection and the equation of the mirror line. As with previous transformations, tracing paper is a useful tool. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may not use the perpendicular distance between vertices and a diagonal mirror line. • Students may draw an incorrect reflection when a shape crosses one of the axes. • Students may incorrectly plot lines of the form y = a and x = b, resulting in an incorrect reflection. • Students may use non-mathematical vocabulary to describe a reflection, such as “flip” or “mirror”, rather than “reflect”. baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this extend step, students consolidate their understanding of reflections, translations, rotations and enlargements, applying a series of transformations to a shape. This step provides opportunities for students to discuss misconceptions or errors related to each of the four transformations. Highlight that changing the order of transformations can affect the final image. As with previous steps, model different transformations to students. Once confident, students could be encouraged to consider whether a series of transformations can sometimes be represented by a single transformation. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may carry out the transformations in an incorrect order. • Students may misinterpret key information, for example reflecting in the line y = 2 rather than x = 2 • Students may perform a second transformation on the original shape, rather than on the new image. small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Summer__Transformations_4_Enlargement (negative scale factor) (E)
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this extend step, students enlarge shapes using a negative scale factor. Establish that enlarging by a negative scale factor changes both the size and orientation of a shape. Using ray lines to model this process is recommended, as the vertices of the object and image will lie on the same ray lines drawn from the centre of enlargement. Make links between positive and negative scale factors, for example comparing enlargements with scale factors of 2 and −2. If appropriate, students can also investigate negative fractional scale factors. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may enlarge by a positive scale factor, rather than a negative scale factor. • Students may think that a negative scale factor produces a smaller shape. • Students may assume that negative and positive scale factors of the same magnitude, for example 2 and −2, produce identical results. National Curriculum links • Identify and construct congruent triangles, and construct similar shapes by enlargement, with and without coordinate grids Mathematical talk • What is the same and what is different about enlarging by a positive scale factor and enlarging by a negative scale factor? • Does an enlargement always have the same orientation as the original shape? Explain how you know. • Describe what happens when a shape is enlarged by a negative scale factor. • If a point is 4 units to the left of the centre of enlargement, where will its image be when enlarged by a scale factor of −2? • Why is it useful to draw ray lines when enlarging a shape? • In which quadrant will the image be after an enlargement of scale factor , about centre of enlargement ? • How can you check that an enlargement has been drawn accurately? small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Summer__Transformations_5_Describe an enlargement
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students describe enlargements using precise language. Explain that a full description of an enlargement must include both the scale factor of enlargement and the coordinates of the centre of enlargement. Remind students of strategies to calculate the scale factor of enlargement, such as dividing corresponding side lengths and ensuring that they divide the enlarged length by the original length. Model how to construct ray lines to locate the coordinates of the centre of enlargement. If necessary, use sentence stems to support students in structuring their response. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may not describe an enlargement fully, for example only stating the scale factor. • Students may use additive rather than multiplicative reasoning to identify a scale factor. • Students may interpret enlargements incorrectly, for example stating a scale factor of 2 rather than 1 2 • Students may describe an enlargement in the wrong order, for example describing the enlargement of shape B to shape A, rather than shape A to shape B. National Curriculum links • Identify and construct congruent triangles, and construct similar shapes by enlargement, with and without coordinate grids Mathematical talk • What pieces of information do you need to describe an enlargement? • Why is it important to state the coordinates of the centre of enlargement? • Describe how you locate the coordinates of the centre of enlargement. • How can you use pairs of corresponding sides to calculate the scale factor? • How do you know when a shape has been enlarged by a fractional scale factor? • How does an enlargement by a scale factor of 2 differ from an enlargement by a scale factor of 1 2 ? • How could you check that your description of the enlargement is accurate? small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Summer__Transformations_6_Rotation about a point
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students rotate a shape about a specific point. Model the process, clearly demonstrating how each vertex moves around the centre of rotation. Tracing paper is a useful tool for students, enabling them to mark both the object and the centre of rotation before physically rotating the shape. Encourage the use of a “north” arrow or similar reference line to support accurate turns of 90°, 180° and 270°. Highlight that rotations can be clockwise or anticlockwise and emphasise that the object and its image are always congruent, having the same size and shape, but in different orientations. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may rotate a shape about the origin rather than the stated centre of rotation. • Students may rotate a shape in the wrong direction. • Students may not rotate the correct number of degrees, for example rotating 180°, rather than 90°. • Students may not draw the image congruent to the original shape. Year 9_13-14_Summer__Transformations_9_Describe a translation
baseline_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students describe a translation using a column vector. Encourage students to identify a pair of corresponding vertices, then model how to calculate the horizontal and vertical movements needed to map one onto the other. Reinforce that the order is important, with the horizontal movement being written as the top value in the vector and the vertical movement below. Emphasise that the same vector applies to every vertex of the shape, not just the pair chosen.
